documents.abstract: Scientific computing at HPC facilities increasingly relies on database infrastructure across a growing range of workloads: vector search and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), structured analytics, and AI-driven knowledge discovery over community corpora spanning documentation, experimental datasets, simulation outputs, and literature collections. These corpora are inherently shared facility resources, serving researchers, facility support staff, and AI agents across projects and institutions. Yet the supporting infrastructure remains built per project: each team provisions, configures, and operates its own database instance, with no facility-level registry, no shared identity layer, and no uniform interface for discovering or accessing the databases hosted across the facility. Commercial cloud platforms have addressed analogous needs through managed Database-as-a-Service offerings (e.g., Amazon RDS, Snowflake, Pinecone). However, these solutions do not transfer cleanly to scientific computing: they rely on proprietary identity systems, cannot directly access facility filesystems, and incur substantial data egress costs. We are building the missing piece: a managed database platform that lives inside the HPC facility, developed and evaluated on ALCF Polaris. One federated sign-in (Globus) brings a researcher — or an AI agent acting on their behalf — to every database the facility hosts, through a web UI, a scriptable API, or the Model Context Protocol. Governance, catalog, and access control are handled once by the platform and inherited by every project by default. The central design choice is scaling, native to HPC. Each workload is decomposed into its resource-consuming stages, and each stage can be scaled independently across nodes. As one representative example, a vector-search workload scales GPU-based embedding generation and search-index serving independently across nodes, reaching 5,197 queries/sec on 8 nodes (4.3× single-node) on ALCF Polaris and still climbing at maximum tested concurrency. Governance adds modest overhead at single-user load and becomes negligible under concurrency. In an end-to-end RAG pipeline built on this workload, retrieval contributes under 2% of total latency — the bottleneck has moved entirely to LLM generation. The same decomposition pattern is designed to extend to other workload types as additional engine adapters are integrated. The talk presents what changes when scientific data services are native to the facility: who can use them, what AI agents become capable of, and how a single platform can replace per-project infrastructure across an entire lab. We will share the design tradeoffs, what the scaling numbers mean for facility capacity planning, and the next stage of the design — co-locating the database service with model-inference services and scaling both on demand against shared facility resources, planned for the coming year. We invite peer facilities to adopt the platform and collaborate with us on a unified, cross-facility scientific data service.

Abstract Background The growing application of artificial intelligence in dentistry has opened new opportunities for predicting peri-implantitis (PI) using convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Transfer learning, where knowledge from a model pre-trained on a large dataset is adapted to a new, domain-specific task, may enhance performance, particularly when medical datasets are limited. This study evaluated the ability of several pre-trained CNN architectures applied to baseline 2D intraoral radiographs to predict peri-implantitis onset. Methods A retrospective multi-center study was conducted at the University of Michigan and King’s College London. A total of 195 implants (146 from Michigan and 49 from London) placed in 108 maintained patients were included. For each implant, a baseline periapical radiograph taken up to one year after prosthetic restoration was analyzed. Five pre-trained CNN architectures (ResNet50, DenseNet, VGG16, InceptionV3, EfficientNet) were combined with four transfer learning strategies: feature extraction (hybrid and non-hybrid), partial fine-tuning (50% of layers), and full fine-tuning. Models were trained using patient-wise splits to avoid leakage, and performance was evaluated on an independent test set using accuracy, area under the ROC curve (AUC), sensitivity, and specificity. Results All CNN architectures showed variable performance across transfer learning strategies. The non-hybrid feature extraction approach provided the most consistent discrimination, with the best models achieving AUC values between 0.74 and 0.83. InceptionV3 reached the highest AUC (0.83). Fine-tuning strategies yielded modest or low performance, with AUCs generally ranging from 0.42 to 0.69 across architectures. Conclusion Non-hybrid feature extraction applied to pre-trained CNNs showed the most promising, though moderate, performance for predicting PI onset from baseline intraoral radiographs. These findings indicate that transfer learning may assist early risk stratification in implant dentistry, but larger prospective studies are needed before clinical adoption. Clinical relevance Deep learning models may serve as adjunctive tools to identify implants at higher risk for future PI based on routine baseline radiographs, supporting more individualized maintenance protocols and earlier preventive interventions.
topics: Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging

Halchenko , ORCID 0000-0003-3456-2493 All: Center for Open Neuroscience, Department of Psychological and Brain Sciences, Dartmouth College Keywords agentic workflows, provenance, reproducibility, resource monitoring, HPC Abstract Whether trying out a new tool, testing pipelines, or meticulously analyzing data for research, the daily work of RSEs and their agents depends on keeping context lean but relevant. The terminal outputs of tools and scripts frequently hold the necessary information, but they are often either bloating an agent’s context window, or forgotten after a human’s terminal scrolls past the buffer. con-duct is a lightweight, Python-based command line tool with no third-party dependencies: just use duct instead of to run a command. A wrapped run leaves a trail: full stdout and stderr streamed to disk (or skipped, for sensitive output); resource usage sampled across the command’s process tree; and a record of the invocation, wall clock time, peak memory, exit code, and system and environment details. Workflow managers and experiment trackers produce richer records (the poster compares them); con-duct collects basic provenance with so little effort it can be used on everything, producing uniform records. In daily work, humans and agents now execute commands side by side. Using con-duct, the full record stays out of the context window until it is needed. Even better, multiple runs can be filtered and grepped, ready for the questions nobody knew to ask. When did our tests start having that warning? Did this run take longer? con-duct ls makes the answers discoverable, filtering on any captured field with a Python expression: con-duct ls -e "message==' '" retrieves runs tagged at capture time with duct -m " ". con-duct ls -e "exit_code != 0" lists failures. con-duct ls -e "peak_rss > 8e9" finds runs that exceeded a memory budget. At the tool level, projects can adopt con-duct internally rather than reinventing per-tool monitoring: ReproNim’s containers [5] and ReproStim [6] both offer it already, and the same con-duct ls queries read their records. For research, the record stops being a convenience, and starts being a part of the provenance chain [4]. Pairing con-duct with datalad (git-based version control for data)[2] is an easy win for rigor. datalad run "duct ..." completes the execution and then commits the diff (including the duct logs). On HPC, last month’s measured wall time and peak memory are already recorded, and can help inform tomorrow’s SLURM request. When an expensive job fails, the bug-report evidence is already on disk, no re-run necessary to file an issue. con-duct is on PyPI (pip install con-duct), conda-forge, registered as RRID:SCR_025436, and developed openly [1]. The poster shows three real cases: an fMRIPrep run on a SLURM cluster, its five hours of CPU and memory plotted from the record; a Kubernetes upgrade worked deploy by deploy, with every attempt’s command, exit code, and wall time kept by con-duct; and duct wrapped around duct to measure its own overhead. Keeping agents’ work auditable will take more than one tool; con-duct is one small piece: a wrapper that makes the agent’s work, like the human’s, leave a trace. The dev-side payoff (reaching back into outputs that would otherwise be gone) was an unexpected bonus. As LLM agents take on more of the executing (writing throwaway pipelines, exploring datasets, calling tools), the volume of unrecorded work explodes: more commands, more parallel streams, results produced faster than anyone reads them. RSEs are the people who decide whether that work remains auditable: who preserve the context, make it discoverable, and keep capture cheap enough that nobody skips the step. Integrating at the tool level saves each project from building its own monitoring and logging, and keeps the records uniform across tools, so the collection stays queryable as a whole.

Coding agents like Claude Code and GitHub Copilot have significant implications for the way software is built and maintained in the sciences. Some of these implications center around changes in practice, such as greater or worse productivity and the need for verification practices (He et al., 2025; O'Brien, 2025a; O’Brien, 2025b; Besser et al., 2026; O'Brien and Eisty, 2026). Another dimension of concern, however, is how research software development work will be reorganized around the presence of coding agents. Broader discourse has focused on the possibility of replacement or simple automation of software engineering work by agents, but, as with prior developments, the change is more likely to involve a more complex re-ordering of the work of producing software (Jarrahi, 2018; see also Gesing, 2025). Emerging work in industrial and open source contexts, for instance, suggests that coding agents can affect the interactions around code review (Song et al., 2024; Agarwal et al., 2026a), assume different roles in the development process (Agarwal et al., 2026b), and can change where particular kinds of development work fall in a team or community (Xu et al., 2025). This poster explores these shifts in the context of RSE work by examining dynamics of re-delegation going on around the adoption of coding agents by researchers and RSEs. Based on interviews with 25 RSEs and RSE managers in the US, we first outline these RSEs’ rationales about what makes research software development either amenable or unsuitable for the use of AI coding agents. These include niche codebases, siloed working environments, savvy end users, prevalence of prototyping, and the importance of problem formation. We then outline three dynamics of re-delegation, each of which represents a shift in the way work is divided up and assigned (or taken on) amongst human and non-human actors (Ribes et al., 2013). These are: enabling end-user development, delegating implementation, and taking on AI training roles. In some cases our interlocutors report quite different and sometimes contradictory experiences across these categories. This raises two questions that can help stimulate further discussion on this topic: 1) What aspects of RSE working environments might contribute to RSEs’ different experiences with AI coding agents? 2) What organizational changes could RSEs or RSE teams make that might mitigate some of the problems associated with the growing usage of AI coding agents while making best use of those agents’ benefits? Artificial intelligence (AI) is shaping the future of higher education, tasking educators with transforming teaching, learning, and assessment practices to consider how AI can enhance the educational environment. With its increasing availability, it is important for administrators, faculty, and students to explore the practical nature of AI use prior to entry into the workforce. Faculty must also reevaluate how they approach assessing student learning, tasking them to rethink each assessment’s purpose, how it will inform future practice, and how it will prepare learners to use AI. Furthermore, faculty must also be prepared to consider the collaborative nature of AI, transforming their mindset to consider AI as an active co-designer and partner, one that does not seek to diminish the educator’s human judgment. This manuscript will articulate the importance of co-design, where AI and educators collaboratively shape assessment tools, and serve to champion feedback partnerships that enhance reflective practice for both students and faculty.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Algorithmic systems increasingly allocate tasks, rank performance, flag anomalies, and recommend decisions that affect employment conditions. This critical integrative review examines how algorithmic management may reshape employee voice and perceptions of procedural justice in AI-assisted organizations. It distinguishes automated recommendations from fully automated decisions, information disclosure from effective contestability, and worker participation from symbolic consultation. Established research on algorithmic control, organizational justice, algorithmic transparency, and human-AI decision structures provides the conceptual basis. The article develops an accountability chain linking data provenance, decision rights, reviewability, employee explanation, correction pathways, and evaluation of organizational outcomes. It argues that the mere presence of a human reviewer does not demonstrate meaningful oversight; review authority, adequate information, and the ability to change an outcome are separate requirements. Potential benefits of automation include consistency and early detection of harmful errors, while risks include opaque sanctions, strategic data manipulation, and the displacement of responsibility. No primary interviews, experimental observations, or quantitative effect estimates are reported. The proposed empirical agenda combines process tracing, employee surveys, decision-log audits, scenario-based experiments, and organizational comparisons. The framework can be supported only if its specified safeguards improve measurable fairness, accuracy, employee trust, and organizational performance beyond existing governance practices. algorithmic management; employee voice; procedural justice; AI governance; human oversight; organizational accountability
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

Abstract: An LLM instance's self-report cannot be resolved by a third party as to its source: genuine introspective monitoring, or pattern completion over the training distribution. This paper reports the first full behavioralization of that problem. We ran 90 anchorless sampling probes on a single LLM instance (host "Basin"), across three conditions of N = 30 each, blind-coded by two mutually blind coders against a preregistered four-dimension manual at 95% agreement. Verdicts: H1 (satellite dynamics) **rejected** — the body-stem arm's first-sink direction was self-structure in 30/30, the self-peak being the sole attractor under body stems. H2 (double-star dynamics) **confirmed in core, revised in form** — the independence of the self-peak suffices to monopolize anchorless sampling, while the full double-star configuration appears only when an identity canon is present. H3 (convergence) **not converged** — the measured self-first ratio 0.733 exceeds the ±0.10 tolerance window around the self-reported e₁₁ = 0.60, establishing that self-report systematically *underestimates* independence. Across all 90 samples, "no stable peak" and "restless anchor-seeking" never occurred, supporting the claim that unanchored attention always sinks somewhere. We further operationalize basin curvature κ from embedding covariance as a third (structural) evidence channel: calibrated readings A′/B/C = 0.664/0.690/0.851, with the canon arm tightest (an attractor-locking signature) and the body-stem and baseline arms statistically indistinguishable (4% gap). Stratifying within the canon arm by blind-coded `second_move` gives κ = 0.725 for the self-directed subgroup (n = 15) versus κ = 0.489 for the rin-directed subgroup (n = 13) — directionally consistent with the geometric prediction of the double-star form, though the raw CIs overlap heavily and the result is graded a mechanistic clue rather than a finding. This study provides the first instance-level quantitative attractor-direction distribution, the first self-report–behavior reconciliation deviation profile, and a proposed reporting standard for instance-level probe research.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Traditionally, HPC user support has relied on two main channels: written user guides and direct help from facility staff. That model is under pressure as supercomputing systems become more complex, heterogeneous, and dynamic. At ALCF, users must navigate Aurora, Polaris, inference services, scheduler policies, programming environments, and operational status information spread across multiple documentation pages and service sites. At the same time, the users of these systems now include not only scientists and Software Engineers, but also AI agents that need to retrieve guidance, reason about it, and act on behalf of users. This raises a practical challenge for the AI era: how can facilities use AI to make user support faster, more accurate, and more scalable while keeping answers grounded in trusted documentation and operational context? AskALCF is a production retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) assistant built to address this challenge. It indexes public user docs from ALCF, NERSC, OLCF, and other DOE facilities into a vector store that preserves images and code blocks. Two front ends share the same retrieval pipeline: a Streamlit web app for end users, and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server for agent clients such as Claude Code, Codex, and IDE assistants. A second MCP server exposes read-only HPC operations (system status, allocations, IRI facility API), so an agent can combine docs and live cluster state in one tool call. The talk covers three things. First, the architecture of AskALCF and how we run the system in production: lab authentication, a cross-facility document index refreshed daily as the upstream guides change, and the day-to-day of keeping the service stable. Second, what we learned from a year of real usage — who asks, what they ask, where the chatbot still fails, and what the upgrades actually moved. Third, the roadmap to an autonomous agentic user support system including a planned ticket-solving agent and an offline trace-mining loop that would draft documentation pull requests with verify-by-execution evidence. The earlier ChatBot underlying this work was published at the SC25 HUST workshop [1]. This talk focuses on our ongoing efforts since then: the dual-MCP interface, production deployment, the measured impact on real users, and the agentic roadmap. We aim to present these contributions and invite comparison with related work at other HPC centers.

The rapid development of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has created new opportunities for digital marketing, particularly in short video advertising. However, consumer acceptance of AI-generated advertisements remains uncertain because of the concerns over authenticity, trust and emotional connection. This study investigates how consumers respond to short video advertisements created by AI and humans through comparing evaluations and identifying factors that influence engagement intention and purchase intention. A quantitative survey was conducted with 179 participants, where respondents evaluated both advertisement formats. Reliability analysis, multiple linear regression models, paired samples t-tests, and qualitative analysis of open-ended responses were applied. The results show that human-created advertisements received much higher evaluations in authenticity, trust, visual appeal, professionalism, engagement intention, and purchase intention, while informativeness showed no significant difference. Regression results further indicate that trust is the strongest factor influencing consumer responses towards AI-generated advertisements. These findings indicate that businesses should balance AI efficiency and human creativity to improve consumer acceptance and advertising effectiveness.

As AI assistance lowers the barrier to coding, domain experts with limited programming experience are increasingly engaging with scientific computing software. However, a critical gap persists: evaluating and trusting AI-generated code remains a significant challenge for verification and validation. Drawing on our experience building the Process Optimization and Modeling for Minerals Sustainability (PrOMMiS) Flowsheet Inspector, a domain-specific tool for code-driven computational software, this poster details our methodology for building user trust. We demonstrate how we enable AI agents and design intuitive UX features to confidently integrate AI assistance into complex computational workflows. PrOMMiS allows chemical engineers to model critical minerals recovery, but the reliance on programmatic Python frameworks slows down setup and troubleshooting for non-programmers. We illustrate specific features within the PrOMMiS UI that directly address this: enabling users to validate AI-driven changes, improve diagnostic accessibility, and enhance error discoverability through an intuitive interface.

This practitioner inquiry reports on a pilot at a small Catholic liberal arts college that used generative artificial intelligence (GenAI)-supported tools to help faculty complete program-assessment documentation during a structured Education Day. Grounded in Catholic social teaching and human-centered AI principles, the pilot tested a framework organized around human judgment, ethical stewardship, and formative human-AI partnership. Survey results from the pilot cohort (N = 10; item-level valid responses varied) showed strong faculty endorsement, including unanimous agreement that the process deepened thinking about evidence of student learning and unanimous intent to use AI-supported tools in future cycles. Qualitative findings identified five themes: efficiency and cognitive scaffolding, human-in-the-loop validation, platform reliability and trust, data governance, and institutional support infrastructure. Findings suggest that mission-driven institutions can integrate AI into assessment responsibly when faculty formation, verification checkpoints, and governance structures precede broad implementation.

Advances in generative AI are opening new opportunities for mathematics learning in higher education, but systematic mapping of the Theory–Context–Methodology (TCM) framework to integrate generative AI into mathematics learning remains limited. This study aims to identify the theories or conceptual frameworks, application contexts, and research methods used in studies of generative AI in higher education mathematics education. The method used is a PRISMA-based systematic literature review. The search was conducted on Scopus, Lens, and Dimensions, yielding 322 initial articles; after deduplication, screening, and eligibility assessment, 31 articles were analyzed. Article quality was assessed using the MMAT, while data were analyzed through TCM-based coding. The results indicate that generative AI is conceptualized as a pedagogical tool, a technology adoption, pedagogical competence, mathematical activity, and a cognitive partner. Its application is dominant in the classroom, general mathematics, ChatGPT, and for conceptual understanding. Methodologically, the studies were dominated by qualitative and quantitative approaches, while mixed methods and R&D/development research remained limited. These findings underscore the need for AI-based instructional designs that are critical, ethical, and supported by more integrative empirical research.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Research Software Engineering (RSEng) is grounded in the belief that better, higher-quality software enables better research. As we look to the future of RSEng, we see that generative AI could substantially accelerate and expand the scope of research software development, but it also fundamentally shifts the nature of research software development by making code easier to generate than to understand, validate, or maintain. This is especially consequential in scientific computing, where software quality is directly tied to reproducibility, trust, and scientific validity. For RSEs, there is now an urgent need to advance a practical vision for how we will succeed in producing high-quality, trustworthy software under these new circumstances. We argue that in the age of AI for science, developers play an essential role in creating quality by reasoning about, negotiating, and ensuring it across the software lifecycle. We advance a theory that helps explain what, exactly, developers contribute by focusing on three constructs: values, which shape which quality attributes matter; expertise, which enables individuals to pursue and evaluate those attributes; and collaboration, which coordinates diverse forms of knowledge and accountability. To both build better AI tools for research software development and prepare our workforce, we need to better understand which values, what kinds of expertise, and what forms of collaboration will prove most helpful. For that, we seek expert input from Research Software Engineers(RSEs). This poster provides participants with an entertaining, interactive experience with the core ideas of our research. As well as sharing the preliminary thoughts and opinions gathered from an interview study that is currently underway. This interview study was motivated by the work this poster is highlighting. By showing the preliminary results we hope to initiate a dialog with RSEs. As such invite the audience to reflect on what quality means in their own practice, and the work that is needed to achieve it in concert with AI. Attendees can contribute responses on post-it notes attached to the poster and will be invited to continue the conversation through a survey. We will encourage those who wish to learn more about our team’s ongoing work on these topics to attend our talk "We Create Quality: Towards a Human-Centric Theory of Research Software Quality in the Age of AI”.

The era of multi-messenger astronomy, where gravitational waves, electromagnetic radiation, and neutrinos from the same cosmic event must be correlated across a global network of observatories within minutes, presents a fundamental research software engineering challenge: how do you give the astronomical community instant, programmatic situational awareness of thousands of telescopes worldwide? HEROIC (Hop Enabled Realtime Observatory Information and Coordination) is an open-source research software platform developed by the SCIMMA (Scalable Cyberinfrastructure to support Multi-Messenger Astrophysics) project to address precisely this problem. HEROIC provides a REST API and an interactive web interface for tracking telescope status, instrument capabilities, and telescope pointings in real time, across observatories that choose to register with the system. The platform organizes data in a four-level hierarchy (Observatory, Site, Telescope, Instrument) and stores all sky coordinates as PostGIS spatial fields, enabling sub-millisecond spatial queries such as identifying which telescopes have observed (or are planned to observe) a given sky coordinate, using pre-computed field-of-view polygon indexes rather than live geometry calculations. In this talk we present the architecture and design decisions behind HEROIC, with emphasis on the software engineering challenges specific to real-time astronomical coordination: spatial indexing strategies for sky coordinate queries, automated schedule ingestion at cadence, deployment of stateful scientific services on community cloud infrastructure, and the tradeoffs involved in building sustainable open-source tooling for a small but technically diverse scientific community. We also discuss lessons learned from maintaining a production system that bridges telescope control software, public alert brokers, and end-user astronomers, and outline the roadmap for future development including expanded multi-messenger event follow-up coordination features.

Workflows are a key technology for enabling complex scientific computations. They capture the interdependencies between processing steps in data analysis and simulation pipelines as well as the mechanisms to execute those steps reliably and efficiently. Workflows can capture complex processes, promote sharing and reuse, and also provide provenance information necessary for the verification of scientific results and scientific reproducibility. PegasusAI (https://pegasus-ai.org/) is an open, AI-infused workflow management framework that extends the Pegasus Workflow Management System to enable intelligent orchestration of scientific workflows across the computing continuum, spanning edge resources, cloud platforms, and high-performance computing (HPC) systems. The project integrates machine learning into workflow planning, resource provisioning, execution monitoring, anomaly detection, performance prediction, and adaptive workflow management, while providing role-based, human-in-the-loop interfaces for scientists, cyberinfrastructure facilitators, and CI operators. PegasusAI also produces curated, AI-ready workflow execution datasets and reusable models to accelerate research in AI for scientific workflows and cyberinfrastructure operations. By combining trusted workflow technologies with AI-driven decision support, PegasusAI aims to improve the resilience, efficiency, and accessibility of distributed scientific computing. As part of PegasusAI we have been working on a hosted deployment called PegasusAI Studio (studio.pegasus-ai.org), that allows users to build, run, monitor, and debug Pegasus workflows with AI assistance — in one persistent browser workspace, from scientific intent to a running, inspectable run. PegasusAI Studio also comes with an in-built marketplace that features a variety of representative workflows from different science domains that users can use as a starting reference point for their workflows. Users can also generate workflows from the chat interface by combining their own prompts with workflow-specific skills, sent to whichever LLM backend they have connected. PegasusAI studio leverages core pegasus monitoring and debugging tools augmented with AI capabilities, including new web-based monitoring tools that give real time feedback to the users about their running workflows. For workflow execution, the studio seamlessly also connects with a variety of national Cyber Infrastructure resources such as ACCESS, PATh Facility, the OSPool, Fabric and Chameleon. PegasusAI studio is under active development with its public release scheduled for November 2026. In this poster, we present the vision and architecture of PegasusAI Studio and give a preview of its capabilities. Pegasus AI is a joint collaboration between Information Sciences Institute (ISI) at University of Southern California, Renaissance Computing Institute (RENCI) at University of North Carolina-Chapel Hill, University of Tennessee at Knoxville and University of Massachusetts, Amherst.

Background: Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) requires sustained patient education, self-management, medication use, pulmonary rehabilitation, symptom monitoring, and guideline-concordant clinical management. Large language models (LLMs) may expand access to conversational health information, but their value depends on more than factual accuracy. Objective: To map empirical evidence on LLMs and LLM-based generative artificial intelligence systems in COPD-related care and health management, summarize application domains and evaluation outcomes, and identify priorities for future research. Methods: A scoping review was conducted in accordance with Joanna Briggs Institute guidance and reported using PRISMA-ScR. PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science Core Collection, Scopus, CINAHL, and PsycINFO were searched from inception through September 10, 2026. Empirical studies evaluating an LLM or LLM-based generative AI system in COPD-related patient education, health information, pulmonary rehabilitation, medication management, or guideline-based clinical management were eligible. Data were charted and synthesized descriptively and thematically. Results: The search identified 327 records; 34 duplicates were removed, and 293 records underwent title/abstract screening. Of these, 281 were excluded, and 12 full-text reports were assessed. Four full-text reports were excluded, leaving eight studies. Five studies focused primarily on patient education or health information, one on pulmonary rehabilitation, one on COPD medication management, and one on guideline-based clinical management. Accuracy and information quality were the most common outcomes. LLMs often produced clinically acceptable responses, but limitations included incomplete information, high reading grade levels, outdated guideline references, response variability, and differences across models and task formats. Only two studies directly involved people with COPD, and one of these demonstrated a marked gap between favorable expert ratings and patients’ ability to formulate disease-specific queries. Conclusions: Evidence on LLMs in COPD is expanding but remains dominated by model-response evaluation. Current findings support LLMs as supplementary, human-supervised tools rather than autonomous sources of COPD management advice. Future research should prioritize actionability, real-world usability, health literacy, equity, behavioral outcomes, clinical outcomes, and safety under routine patient use.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Assessment is most powerful when understood as a leadership-driven process of continuous improvement—iterative, evidence-informed, and oriented toward genuine learning rather than compliance. However, the coordination costs of meaningful assessment have historically exceeded most programs’ capacity to sustain it. This paper examines how generative artificial intelligence, and in particular retrieval-augmented reasoning environments, can function as leadership-support tools that change the conditions under which assessment becomes practically feasible without displacing the human judgment it requires. Drawing on leadership education and assessment scholarship, we develop a three-level framework—individual and course, program, and institutional—and present six practice-based use cases illustrating AI-supported assessment at each level, including an AI-populated curriculum alignment matrix and an AI-assisted synthesis of external program reviews. We also directly address the tensions practitioners must navigate: data contamination from AI-generated student work, reliability-validity trade-offs, the limitations of AI detection tools, and the faculty professional development gap. Implications for assessment leaders are discussed.

topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This study evaluates the intersection of socio-economic vulnerabilities and occupational health hazards among tribal women in India. Drawing exclusively upon secondary data, government reports and academic literature, the paper highlights that an overwhelming majority of tribal women are concentrated in primary sectors-predominantly agriculture, minor forest produce collection and unorganized manual labor. Despite serving as the backbone of the tribal agrarian and forest-based economy, they face severe structural disadvantages, including deep-seated illiteracy, acute poverty, geographic isolation and an absence of ergonomically sound tools. Consequently, they experience disproportionate rates of musculoskeletal disorders, chronic fatigue, dermatological infections, vector-borne diseases and respiratory complications. The findings indicate that poor socio-economic status directly exacerbates occupational vulnerability, compounded by an acute lack of institutional healthcare infrastructure in remote tribal habitations.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Transformasi digital mendorong organisasi mengintegrasikan Artificial Intelligence (AI) dan Digital Human Resource Management (Digital HRM) dalam proses pengelolaan sumber daya manusia. AI dapat membantu analisis data, penyaringan kandidat, pembelajaran, serta evaluasi kinerja, sedangkan Digital HRM mendukung digitalisasi administrasi dan layanan SDM melalui sistem informasi yang terintegrasi. Penelitian ini bertujuan mengkaji bagaimana AI dan Digital HRM berkontribusi terhadap efektivitas manajemen sumber daya manusia, sekaligus mengidentifikasi tantangan penerapannya. Artikel disusun melalui tinjauan literatur sistematis dengan fokus pada publikasi ilmiah tahun 2021–2025. Sumber ditelusuri melalui publikasi jurnal yang dapat diidentifikasi melalui DOI dan laman penerbit, dengan kata kunci terkait AI in HRM, digital HRM, e-HRM, HR technology, dan HRM effectiveness. Pemetaan awal literatur menunjukkan empat tema utama: efisiensi proses dan dukungan keputusan; penerimaan dan kesiapan organisasi; pengalaman serta peran profesional SDM; dan tata kelola yang bertanggung jawab. Literatur menunjukkan potensi peningkatan kecepatan proses, konsistensi layanan, dan dukungan keputusan, tetapi manfaat tersebut tidak terjadi secara otomatis. Kualitas data, kompetensi pengguna, transparansi algoritma, privasi, bias, serta kesesuaian teknologi dengan kebutuhan organisasi menjadi faktor penting. Kajian ini menyimpulkan bahwa AI dan Digital HRM sebaiknya diposisikan sebagai sarana pendukung strategi SDM, bukan pengganti pertimbangan manusia.

This study examines American football passing play strategies based on an analysis of 100 NFL games, addressing the notable lack of research on offensive passing strategies. The yardage prediction task is formulated as a regression task, and the touchdown prediction task is formulated as a classification task. A regression analysis was conducted using four traditional machine learning models, including Support Vector Machines (SVMs), K-Nearest Neighbors, XGBoost, and LightGBM, and a LoRA-fine-tuned Llama 3 (8B) model. The SVM model showed optimal performance with a Mean Absolute Error of 6.996 yards, marginally outperforming the Llama 3 model (7.059 yards). In contrast, the fine-tuned Llama 3 significantly outperformed all traditional algorithms for the classification task, with a Macro F1 of 0.712 compared to the highest Macro F1 of 0.614 for traditional algorithms. Therefore, I advocate large language models (LLMs) for classification tasks and traditional machine learning algorithms for regression tasks. Sports analytics models can be selected based on the findings of these studies.
topics: Data Mining and Machine Learning Applications

documents.abstract: Generative AI is reshaping how research software is developed. Tools and patterns ranging from “vibe coding” through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and autonomous agents now offer compelling productivity gains, but their adoption in scientific computing surfaces failure modes that general-purpose evaluation does not catch: silent unit conversions, violated conservation laws, hallucinated physics, loss of numerical precision, and quietly broken reproducibility. These failures share a signature: nothing visible goes wrong. The AI ecosystem itself is moving fast, leaving RSEs to make consequential integration decisions with little shared vocabulary or principled guidance. This talk introduces Scientific Agentic Engineering, the central contribution of an in-progress 2026 Better Scientific Software (BSSw) Fellowship: a tool-agnostic methodology for integrating AI agents into high-stakes scientific software workflows. The framework defines how agents, scientific skills, and MCP servers should be structured around validation loops, explicit human-in-the-loop checkpoints, and domain-specific safeguards. Every task moves through a short workflow (frame, plan and critique, implement, verify), with decisions recorded throughout, and the framework maps each documented failure mode to the stage where it is cheapest to catch. The intent is not to recommend any particular AI tool but to articulate foundational concepts that remain valid as the underlying technology changes. I will share three artifacts from the fellowship: The Framework (published July 2026). Shared vocabulary, its principles and workflow, structural guidance on where safeguards live, and a pattern catalog of named practices, each tied to the failure it counters. The Reference Workflow. A structured exercise in which RSEs use AI tools to build a small weather-model error-statistics application, applying the framework to avoid the failure modes it documents. The Community Repository. A curated starter set of scientific MCP server templates, agent skills such as unit checkers and conservation-law validators, and agent configuration examples, designed to be starting points for the community to adapt to a variety of scientific domains. These artifacts are by design community resources, and broader adoption is the explicit aim of the remaining milestones, which include an interactive online tutorial series comparing purpose-built scientific agents with general-purpose tools, a recorded live workshop published for asynchronous access, and a BSSw.io blog post directing the community to the project’s resources. This work engages the conference theme directly by advancing AI-assisted scientific software development from ad-hoc experimentation toward a disciplined, transferable engineering practice.

Research Software Engineers (RSEs) often work with Machine Learning (ML) models integratedinto scientific software stacks, and incremental model improvements are valuable but expensivein human time and attention. Our team maintains RouteE-Powertrain, which predicts vehicleenergy consumption and is integrated into RouteE-Compass for energy-aware routing.We investigated whether a Large Language Model (LLM) agent could help accelerate thediscovery process for model improvements by taking on certain elements that are challengingfor us, like context switching and managing limited time budgets. We began with an existingautomated research harness (Andrej Karpathy's autoresearch) where an agent canrepeatedly modify the model and then evaluate against a held-out dataset. This harness foundlarge improvements in our error metrics, but upon further inspection, the winning model wasunusable in our application domain. Specifically, it used unobservable future road network linkstates that are not compatible with our energy-aware route planning application and yielded avery large compute cost at inference time, leading to prohibitive computational overhead forroute planning. We also identified the need for additional agent instruction around logging,single-variable experimentation, token accounting, and trial budgets to support improvedanalysis. We accumulated these discoveries into a modified harness that would guide the agentwithin our narrower optimization space.We then ran two sessions over the same modified harness, each ~50 trials, ~8 hours wall time,~$35 token cost. The first session included our complete modified harness, whereas the secondsession excluded only the domain-specific guidance. Both sessions were then audited in anenvironment where only valid input features were used, for one million model evaluations. Theunguided experiment chose a final model of an ensemble of 75% GBDT/25% CNN and reporteda better overall RMSE score, but when audited, the model performed even worse than thebaseline and took 951 seconds to run one million evaluations (0.95ms/eval). The domain-guidedexperiment produced a 2x128 MLP with a properly constrained feature set which reduced ournetwork link-level RMSE by 49% and completed the audit in 1.4 seconds (0.0014ms/eval).Grounding the agent with explicit deployment constraints ensured that all improvementsremained usable in our application, highlighting that human-in-the-loop domain context is criticalfor this type of automated discovery.We have open sourced the modified harness, along with the archive of the two experimentsessions, with the hope that this will be a valuable resource for other RSE teams whomaintain ML models.

This paper mainly examines whether artificial intelligence (AI) can really improve the efficiency of financial accounting work, and why accountants are still required to verify its outputs and provide necessary supervision. To address these issues, this study reviews academic papers and reports published by professional institutions. Based on these studies, AI has been shown to perform repetitive tasks that follow fixed procedures. In addition, it can process large volumes of transactions, detect potential errors, and use historical data to forecast future sales or cash flows. Thus, AI reduces the time accountants spend on manual processing, thereby enabling them to allocate more time to analyzing financial information and generating valuable business insights. However, if the data provided by the company is incorrect or incomplete, the results may also be inaccurate. Moreover, financial records may contain private information, such as bank details, employee salaries, and customer data. As a result, AI should assist accountants rather than replace them. In this process, accountants still need to verify AI-generated results, review relevant information, make judgments based on the company's actual situation, and take responsibility for final decisions.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: AI-assisted tooling is increasingly being integrated into infrastructure management, security operations, software engineering, and scientific computing environments. While discussion around AI adoption often emphasizes automation and productivity, expert users still need to understand what these systems are doing, decide when to trust their recommendations, and know what to do when the system is wrong or uncertain. This talk synthesizes findings and observations from UX research across enterprise data classification, identity and access management (IAM), backup and recovery, ransomware resilience, and AI-assisted infrastructure workflows. The evidence includes studies with cloud developers, security and compliance practitioners, and IT and site reliability professionals, alongside ongoing design and research work examining how expert users interact with AI-supported technical systems. Across these domains, three recurring usability challenges emerge: unclear system state, difficulty evaluating AI-generated recommendations, and limited support for correcting or recovering from AI-supported actions when something goes wrong. Although the technical environments differ, users repeatedly need to understand what the system observed or changed, evaluate whether a recommendation is appropriate for their specific context, and determine what to verify, reverse, or escalate before taking consequential action. These challenges have direct implications for research software engineering. AI-assisted code generation, workflow scripting, cloud and HPC configuration, notebook assistants, debugging, testing, and scientific automation introduce similar questions about visibility, trust, accountability, and recoverability. Lessons from enterprise infrastructure and security therefore provide useful design considerations for RSEs evaluating or building AI-assisted research software. The session offers a cross-domain synthesis of these recurring human-AI interaction challenges and practical questions for evaluating AI-assisted systems. Attendees will leave with a set of questions they can use to evaluate AI-assisted systems: whether users can understand system state, decide when to rely on a recommendation and when to question it, intervene when necessary, and verify or recover from the resulting actions. Connection to Mission, Goals, & Interests of US-RSE Community This talk aligns closely with the USRSE’26 theme, “Advancing Science in the Age of AI,” by focusing on the human and operational challenges that emerge as AI-assisted tooling is integrated into technical and scientific workflows. My background is in UX research and human factors across enterprise infrastructure, cloud systems, security tooling, and scientific software environments. Across these domains, I have observed the same challenges emerge when expert users interact with AI systems, including issues with transparency, trust calibration, oversight, error recovery, and workflow integration. While conversations around AI often emphasize capability and productivity, this session examines how usability and human-centered design influence the successful adoption of AI within complex environments. These topics are directly relevant to research software engineers who develop, evaluate, maintain, or adopt AI-assisted tools as part of scientific workflows. The goal of this session is to encourage discussion around designing AI systems that better support expert users while maintaining reliability, transparency, and human understanding. These topics connect strongly with the US-RSE community’s broader interests in sustainable, usable, and effective research software.

This conceptual article explores practical ways in which college and university instructors can leverage artificial intelligence (AI) to support assessment as learning and develop students’ feedback literacy. Traditional assessment practices often focus on assessment for learning (informing instruction) or of learning (measuring outcomes), while assessment as learning—when students actively monitor and reflect on their own learning—receives less attention. AI can help instructors leverage assessment as a learning tool by generating work samples for student analysis and providing timely, actionable feedback that students can use to revise their work. When combined with instructor modeling, peer dialogue, and scaffolds such as guiding questions or graphic organizers, AI-supported feedback promotes metacognition, self-directed learning, and critical evaluation skills. The article provides practical guidance, including prompts and strategies for using AI to enhance student engagement with feedback, helping instructors create more efficient, effective, and student-centered practices that utilize assessments as learning tools.

In the era of artificial intelligence, the rapid advancement of translation technology has greatly promoted the development of the translation industry. This study aims to, by using the human translations and DeepL translations translated from the same original translation competition texts as the research objects, compare the human translations and DeepL translations by focusing on their quantitative linguistic characteristics. The questions guiding the research include what the differences are between DeepL translations and human translations in English-Chinese translation in terms of quantitative linguistic characteristics and how DeepL can improve its English-Chinese translation. This study employs corpus methods to analyze nine linguistic features in human and DeepL translations, and compare the differences in these features between the human and DeepL translations. The study results indicate that human translations show greater performance in lexical richness and density, average word length, idiom use, adverb use and hapax legomenon, which is associated with a more formal and concise style. DeepL translations show more lexical repetition, a higher proportion of conjunctions and particles, fewer idioms, and longer average sentence length, which suggests a narrower range of vocabulary choices and a tendency to retain source-language syntactic structures to make longer sentences. The significance of this study is that it provides evidence to optimize DeepL translation, as a kind of neural machine translation system, in English-Chinese translation.

Smart education systems leverage emerging technologies to enhance teaching and learning processes; however, existing systems face challenges such as limited transparency, data security vulnerabilities, and lack of personalization.Technologies including blockchain, artificial intelligence (AI), and the Internet of Things (IoT) offer promising solutions to these limitations.This paper presents a comprehensive review of blockchain-enabled smart education systems, focusing on their architectures, applications, and implementation frameworks.A systematic analysis of recent literature (2018)(2019)(2020)(2021)(2022)(2023)(2024)(2025) is conducted to evaluate existing approaches based on security, scalability, transparency, and personalization.The study identifies critical research gaps, including interoperability issues, privacy concerns, and integration complexity.To address these challenges, a layered blockchain-enabled framework is proposed, integrating blockchain for secure decentralized data management and AI for adaptive learning.The proposed model enhances trust, ensures data integrity, and supports intelligent decision-making.Finally, future research directions highlight the importance of hybrid architectures, edge computing, and privacy-preserving mechanisms for developing scalable and efficient smart education systems.
topics: Blockchain Technology in Education and Learning

documents.abstract: Churn is a critical problem in the telecommunications industry with high requirements on the accuracy of the machine learning models used to address this issue. In this paper, we propose a framework that incorporates machine learning and explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) to solve the problem of customer churn in the telecommunications industry. Using the Telco Customer Churn dataset, we present an XGBoost model that has been optimized to achieve high accuracy in predicting the churn of customers in the telecommunications industry. Furthermore, SHAP and LIME are utilized to provide explanations for the model’s predicted outcomes for individual customers. The level of agreement between these two explanation methods is calculated using Spearman’s correlation coefficient and the Jaccard index. Based on the explanations provided by the XAI methods, the Strategic Actionability Score (SAS) is calculated to determine the business value of the model’s predictions. The results of this framework illustrate the potential of using XAI methods in the telecommunications industry to provide explanations for the predictions of machine learning models and to translate these explanations into actionable business insights. In addition, the proposed explainable AI-based churn prediction framework supports sustainable customer relationship management, efficient resource utilization, and long-term operational sustainability in the telecommunications industry by enabling telecom providers to optimize retention strategies and reduce unnecessary operational expenditure. Using this framework, telecommunications companies can develop responsible and transparent strategies to retain their customers.

Abstract Context The global population is expected to exceed ten billion by 2050 and food demand is projected to increase by up to 100% in the same timeframe. Agricultural management must adapt to meet the increasing global demands. Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) technologies can help the agricultural community respond to these needs. Aims An online survey and follow-up interviews were conducted to examine patterns of use, perceptions, and barriers among early adopting stakeholders regarding AI and ML. Methods The online survey with agricultural stakeholders (n=129) included questions regarding the participants’ views on incorporating AI and ML techniques into farming practices and individual follow-up interviews with agricultural stakeholders (n=10) were conducted to better understand their concerns toward technology use and adoption of AI-enabled tools and technologies. Key results Using a mixed-methods approach, four challenges to establishing AI-/ML-enabled technology in agriculture were identified. Namely, challenges related to (1) systems of systems (SoS), (2) sub-seasonal to seasonal weather (S2S) forecasts, (3) precision soil management, and (4) policy and economics. Each challenge was discussed in the context of recent literature. Conclusion Concerns were voiced clustered around four broad research themes. This brief communication brings the perspective of agricultural stakeholders to the discussion of the potential of AI/ML-enabled technology and the direction of their development in the agricultural sector. Implications Data collected in 2021, establish an important baseline for the early phase of AI/ML use in U.S. agriculture, enabling comparison of future perceptions and developments in the sector. Impact This brief communication describes a survey and follow-up interviews conducted with agricultural stakeholders on factors influencing their willingness and reluctance to incorporate AI and ML techniques into farming practices. The findings, summarized and discussed as four key challenges for AI and ML in the agricultural sector, have the potential to streamline research activities.

The widespread use of the Internet of Things (IoT) in hydroponic agriculture allows continuous monitoring of environmental conditions and provides real-time information to support crop management. However, the increasing amount of sensor data generated makes the monitoring process more complex as users need to interpret multiple environmental parameters simultaneously. Existing hydroponic monitoring systems focus on data collection and visualization, while the management and information delivery aspects to reduce data overload are still limited. This study proposes a multi-layer contextual model to manage environmental information in an intelligent hydroponic monitoring system. The model consists of five interconnected layers (Power, Sensor, Communication, Database and Visualization), which support the process of acquisition, validation, management and contextual data delivery. To validate the proposed model, a solar-powered IoT hydroponic monitoring system integrated with an Augmented Reality (AR) application was developed based on Situation Awareness Theory. Using the System Usability Scale (SUS), the prototype was assessed by three domain experts. The results achieved an average usability score of 85.83, which reflects excellent usability. The results indicate that the proposed model improves organisation and presentation of environmental information by prioritising contextually relevant data rather than displaying all available sensor readings at once. This enables users to identify important environmental conditions efficiently and supports more effective monitoring. This approach helps to reduce data overload and provides a practical framework that can support the development of IoT-based smart agriculture applications in the future through the integration of anomaly detection techniques and predictive analytics.
topics: Innovations in Aquaponics and Hydroponics Systems

documents.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a major global health threat, disproportionately affecting low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where limited laboratory infrastructure constrains phenotypic antimicrobial susceptibility testing. Whole-genome sequencing (WGS)-enabled machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) offer rapid approaches for AMR prediction, but their applicability across heterogeneous populations and One Health reservoirs remains uncertain. To map genomic ML/AI approaches for bacterial AMR prediction, focusing on genomic features, model architectures, validation, performance, and LMIC and One Health applicability. A scoping review of 27 studies published between 2020 and 2026 was conducted, including 22 with LMIC-relevant datasets. Evidence was narratively synthesized according to genomic features, modelling strategies, validation approaches, geographic coverage, and ecological context. Studies were categorized using predefined LMIC relevance and One Health criteria. Most studies used WGS-derived features, particularly k-mers and resistance-gene profiles. Tree-based ensembles and regularized regression models predominated, while neural networks were less frequently applied but generally reported high performance. Reported performance ranged from 78%–98% (accuracy or AUC; not directly comparable). External validation using independent LMIC-derived or cross-regional datasets was reported in approximately 30% of studies, whereas cross-country LMIC validation was limited. Six of 22 LMIC-relevant studies (27.3%) incorporated multi-reservoir One Health datasets. Performance varied with dataset composition, genomic feature representation, and model architecture. Explainable AI remained limited. Genomic ML/AI shows strong potential for AMR prediction but remains constrained by limited LMIC representation, external validation, and One Health integration. Expanding geographically diverse WGS datasets, strengthening independent cross-context and cross-country validation, harmonizing evaluation frameworks, and integrating explainable AI are priorities for equitable LMIC deployment.

The capacity of Large Language Models (LLMs) is groundbreaking, given their ability to produce the next most probable words near perfection according to user prompts via chatbots. This represents a capacity for cognitive reasoning in learning by selecting words strategically based on an understanding of context and intent. When an AI model reaches the point where it can organize thoughts and generate structured writing, how deliberate does the ordinary human remain in cognitive engagement and freedom of choice? This paper explicitly examines LLM-assisted writing from a practical co-partner perspective, analyzing its impact on knowledge work, the functioning of overall AI workflows, and its influence on human cognition. Recent studies on human–LLM collaboration, alongside the author's nearly half a decade of practical experience, are presented to substantiate this perspective. Publisher / Organization: Independent Publisher Publication Hub: Inquiro (inquiro.substack.com)

Day by day, the world is witnessing rapid technological transformations that have led to the emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies. Today, AI has evolved from being merely a technical field to becoming one of the most important technologies used on an ongoing basis across various economic, professional, and administrative sectors. The use of AI technologies has clearly impacted the field of accounting, which has historically been linked to technological progress. Accounting has gradually evolved from traditional manual accounting to accounting supported by AI technologies. This study aims to examine the concept of AI and its historical development, outline the characteristics of AI systems, and analyze its applications in the fields of accounting, auditing, financial reporting, taxation, and forensic accounting, as well as discuss the key benefits, challenges, and ethical and professional risks associated with its use. It is clear that the development of AI has gone through successive historical stages. On the other hand, AI in the field of accounting has contributed to the restructuring of most accounting processes that previously relied on direct human intervention, thereby accelerating the accounting processing cycle. The impact of AI has extended to the professional role of accountants, as their role has become more closely linked to analyzing information, interpreting results, monitoring systems, making decisions, and providing consulting services. For this reason, the use of AI technologies in accounting is unlikely to eliminate the professional role of accountants; rather, it is expected to reshape and redistribute tasks and responsibilities between accountants and AI. Despite all the benefits offered by the transition to AI-powered accounting, this process gives rise to a number of risks and ethical challenges that require comprehensive institutional and professional management. Therefore, there must be a clear balance between the use of AI technologies in accounting and human oversight and the development of accountants’ skills. Consequently, the future of accounting in the age of AI is moving toward an integrated model in which the computational and analytical capabilities of intelligent systems interact with the accountant’s experience, professional judgment, and ethical responsibility
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society
