documents.abstract: Anti-ST2 monoclonal antibodies neutralize the interleukin-33 receptor, blocking a key upstream alarmin signalling pathway implicated in airway inflammation, and represent a biologic class under continued investigation for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) exacerbation reduction, an area with limited targeted biologic options relative to severe asthma. This article uses a hypothetical multinational Phase 2 clinical trial of an anti-ST2 monoclonal antibody candidate, sponsored by a fictional company, to compare the Clinical Trial Application (CTA) process required by Health Canada, the Investigational New Drug (IND) process required by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, and the Clinical Trial Application process required by the European Medicines Agency under Regulation (EU) No 536/2014. As a large-molecule biologic governed by ICH S6(R1) principles rather than the small-molecule nonclinical framework, this candidate illustrates how species-relevant pharmacology and immunogenicity considerations carry through the administrative layer of all three regions even though the core harmonized scientific content, Modules 2 through 5 of the Common Technical Document and their EU IMPD equivalent, remains substantially shared. The article addresses the operational challenges specific to a respiratory biologic program conducted across these three jurisdictions, the ways artificial intelligence tools are used, and can responsibly be used, in preparing and administering this kind of regulatory package, and closes with recommendations for regulatory operations teams managing monoclonal antibody candidates in chronic respiratory disease.Keywords: anti-ST2 monoclonal antibody; chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; Clinical Trial Application; Investigational New Drug; Regulation (EU) No 536/2014; ICH S6(R1); regulatory artificial intelligence

Ataxia telangiectasia and Rad3-related protein (ATR) kinase inhibitors are investigational small molecules that target a central regulator of the cellular DNA damage response, exploiting the observation that tumours carrying certain loss-of-function alterations in DNA damage response pathways may be more vulnerable to ATR inhibition than tumours without these alterations. This article uses a hypothetical multicentre Phase 1/2 clinical trial of an ATR kinase inhibitor candidate, sponsored by a fictional company, to compare the Clinical Trial Application (CTA) process required by Health Canada, the Investigational New Drug (IND) process required by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, and the Clinical Trial Application process required by the European Medicines Agency under Regulation (EU) No 536/2014, using a biomarker-selected advanced solid tumour population as the illustrative scenario. The comparison traces how the Common Technical Document's harmonized Modules 2 through 5 carry the shared scientific case across all three regions while the biomarker selection strategy itself, the companion diagnostic or laboratory-developed test used to identify eligible patients, introduces specific administrative and scientific considerations in each region's review. The article addresses the operational challenges specific to a biomarker-driven oncology program conducted across these three jurisdictions, the ways artificial intelligence tools are used, and can responsibly be used, in preparing and administering this kind of regulatory package, and closes with recommendations for regulatory operations teams managing DNA damage response-targeted oncology candidates across Canada, the United States, and the European Union.Keywords: ATR kinase inhibitor; DNA damage response; biomarker-selected oncology trial; Clinical Trial Application; Investigational New Drug; Regulation (EU) No 536/2014; regulatory artificial intelligence

Bispecific antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) that simultaneously engage two distinct cell-surface receptors and deliver a cytotoxic payload represent one of the more structurally complex biologic modalities currently advancing through oncology development, combining the target-engagement logic of bispecific antibody engineering with the potency and bystander-effect considerations of conventional ADC payload chemistry. This article uses a hypothetical multicentre Phase 1b combination trial of a bispecific ADC candidate in recurrent or metastatic head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, sponsored by a fictional company, to compare the Clinical Trial Application (CTA) process required by Health Canada, the Investigational New Drug (IND) process required by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, and the Clinical Trial Application process required by the European Medicines Agency under Regulation (EU) No 536/2014. The comparison traces how the Common Technical Document's harmonized Modules 2 through 5 carry the shared scientific case for a complex biologic across all three regions, while each jurisdiction's administrative layer, Module 1 in Canada and the United States, Part II of the EU's Clinical Trials Information System filing, imposes region-specific requirements that a sponsor developing a combination-therapy oncology program cannot simply duplicate from one region to the next. The article addresses the particular operational challenges this modality and combination-trial design create, the specific ways artificial intelligence tools are used, and can responsibly be used, in preparing and administering this kind of complex, multi-document regulatory package, and closes with recommendations for regulatory operations teams managing bispecific ADC programs across these three jurisdictions.Keywords: bispecific antibody-drug conjugate; oncology combination therapy; Clinical Trial Application; Investigational New Drug; Regulation (EU) No 536/2014; CTIS; regulatory artificial intelligence

Cardiac myosin inhibitors are a recently established mechanistic class that reduces excess cardiac contractility in obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (oHCM) by allosterically and reversibly modulating myosin motor activity, with the first agent in this class having received FDA approval in late 2025. This article uses a hypothetical new multicentre Phase 2 clinical trial of a follow-on cardiac myosin inhibitor candidate, sponsored by a fictional company unrelated to the approved product's marketing authorization holder, to compare the Clinical Trial Application (CTA) process required by Health Canada, the Investigational New Drug (IND) process required by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, and the Clinical Trial Application process required by the European Medicines Agency under Regulation (EU) No 536/2014. Because an approved product already exists in this class, the comparison pays particular attention to how each region's reviewers are expected to treat the established drug-drug interaction and echocardiographic monitoring precedent from that approved product's development when evaluating a new candidate acting through the same mechanism. The article addresses the operational challenges specific to developing a follow-on candidate in a class with an approved precedent, the ways artificial intelligence tools are used, and can responsibly be used, in preparing and administering this kind of regulatory package, and closes with recommendations for regulatory operations teams managing cardiac myosin inhibitor candidates across these three jurisdictions.Keywords: cardiac myosin inhibitor; obstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy; Clinical Trial Application; Investigational New Drug; Regulation (EU) No 536/2014; echocardiographic monitoring; regulatory artificial intelligence

Cholesteryl ester transfer protein (CETP) inhibitors are a class of oral small-molecule agents under continued clinical development for hypercholesterolemia and mixed dyslipidemia, acting by inhibiting the transfer of cholesteryl esters from high-density lipoprotein to lower-density lipoprotein particles. This article uses a hypothetical multinational Phase 2 clinical trial of a CETP inhibitor candidate, sponsored by a fictional company, to compare the Clinical Trial Application (CTA) process required by Health Canada, the Investigational New Drug (IND) process required by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), and the Clinical Trial Application process required by the European Medicines Agency (EMA) under Regulation (EU) No 536/2014. All three jurisdictions rely on the harmonized Common Technical Document (CTD) structure, under which Modules 2 through 5, covering quality, nonclinical, and clinical evidence, are substantially portable across regions, while Module 1 and its regional equivalents remain jurisdiction-specific. The article presents each region's legal framework, review timeline, and administrative content, develops a three-way comparison table, and then turns to the practical challenges a sponsor managing this triad of filings actually faces and the specific ways artificial intelligence tools are being used, and can responsibly be used, in regulatory document preparation, administration, and quality control across all three jurisdictions. The analysis closes with concrete recommendations for regulatory operations teams managing parallel CETP inhibitor trials, and more generally for any oral small-molecule cardiometabolic candidate filed simultaneously in Canada, the United States, and the European Union.Keywords: CETP inhibitor; dyslipidemia; Clinical Trial Application; Investigational New Drug; Regulation (EU) No 536/2014; Common Technical Document; regulatory artificial intelligence

Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) remains a therapeutic area with a limited number of recently approved mechanisms, and new, orally administered small-molecule candidates acting on central monoaminergic pathways continue to be investigated as alternatives or adjuncts to existing selective serotonin and serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors. This article uses a fully hypothetical new chemical entity and a fictional sponsor to compare the Clinical Trial Application (CTA) process required by Health Canada, the Investigational New Drug (IND) process required by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, and the Clinical Trial Application process required by the European Medicines Agency under Regulation (EU) No 536/2014, using a Phase 2, randomized, placebo-controlled dose-ranging trial in adults with moderate-to-severe GAD as the illustrative scenario. The comparison traces how the Common Technical Document's harmonized Modules 2 through 5 carry the shared scientific case across all three regions, while each jurisdiction's administrative layer imposes distinct requirements, including the heightened attention every region's psychiatry-focused review division gives to suicidality monitoring and central nervous system safety signals for any new anxiolytic candidate. The article addresses the operational challenges specific to a central nervous system program conducted across Canada, the United States, and the European Union, the ways artificial intelligence tools are used, and can responsibly be used, in preparing and administering this kind of regulatory package, and closes with recommendations for regulatory operations teams managing novel psychiatric drug candidates across these three jurisdictions.Keywords: generalized anxiety disorder; central nervous system small molecule; Clinical Trial Application; Investigational New Drug; Regulation (EU) No 536/2014; suicidality monitoring; regulatory artificial intelligence

Oral, nonpeptide small-molecule glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists represent a significant pharmaceutical innovation within an already well-established therapeutic mechanism, offering the metabolic benefits long associated with injectable peptide GLP-1 agonists through a once-daily tablet formulation. This article uses a hypothetical multinational Phase 2 clinical trial of an oral GLP-1 receptor agonist candidate, sponsored by a fictional company, to compare the Clinical Trial Application (CTA) process required by Health Canada, the Investigational New Drug (IND) process required by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, and the Clinical Trial Application process required by the European Medicines Agency under Regulation (EU) No 536/2014. Because this candidate's nonpeptide, small-molecule chemical format places it under each region's conventional small-molecule nonclinical framework rather than the biologics-specific framework governing its peptide-based predecessors, the comparison also addresses a regulatory-classification question of direct practical relevance: how chemical format, not shared pharmacological mechanism, determines which nonclinical and administrative conventions actually apply in each of the three jurisdictions. The article addresses the operational challenges specific to this program, the ways artificial intelligence tools are used, and can responsibly be used, in preparing and administering this kind of regulatory package, and closes with recommendations for regulatory operations teams managing oral metabolic drug candidates across Canada, the United States, and the European Union.Keywords: oral GLP-1 receptor agonist; obesity; type 2 diabetes; Clinical Trial Application; Investigational New Drug; Regulation (EU) No 536/2014; regulatory artificial intelligence

The growing computational demands of artificial intelligence have accelerated interest in optical computing as a high-speed and energy-efficient alternative to conventional electronic hardware. Fourier optical computing provides an important foundation for this field because operations including convolution, correlation, spectral transformation, and certain classes of linear transformation can be implemented through diffraction, interference, and Fourier-domain processing. This review traces the development of optical neural computing from classical 4-f processors and free-space diffractive systems to programmable optical neural networks, integrated photonic accelerators, reservoir-computing platforms, and field-programmable photonic architectures. The underlying physical principles, computational mechanisms, and hardware implementations are systematically examined, with particular attention to reconfigurable photonics, metasurfaces, diffractive deep learning, photonic integrated circuits, and hybrid optical–electronic systems. Emerging applications in computational imaging, autonomous sensing, edge intelligence, high-speed communications, and quantum-enabled information processing are critically discussed alongside challenges related to scalability, programmability, nonlinear computation, training, and system integration. By positioning Fourier optics as a foundational branch within the broader landscape of optical neural computing, this review highlights the convergence of free-space, integrated, programmable, and hybrid photonic technologies toward next-generation artificial-intelligence hardware.

Hepatitis still remains one of the major health issues in the world and is responsible for a significant amount of morbidity and mortality due to diseases related to the liver. Traditional approaches for hepatitis detection are costly, laboratorial, time-consuming, and error-prone. While AI and DL have enhanced medical diagnosis significantly, current models are prone to problems such as overfitting, long convergence period, and lack of generalization, which are primarily associated with inefficiency of hyperparameter optimization. In this research, the authors propose the use of optimized deep learning model based on Chaotic Optimization Algorithm (COA) for hepatitis detection. This approach combines Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) and Deep Neural Network (DNN) models with the application of COA, which allows optimizing such parameters as learning rate, hidden neurons, momentum, and weights initialization. Two publicly available datasets (the Kaggle Hepatitis Dataset and the UCI Hepatitis Dataset) have been used in this research. Data preprocessing steps including handling missing values, encoding, normalization, and splitting data into train and test datasets were applied. The COA-DNN gave results of 85.11% for accuracy, 77.83% for precision, 83.24% for recall, 79.85% for F1 score, and 0.9054 for AUC on the Kaggle dataset compared to the conventional DNN which had an accuracy of 57.45%. For the UCI dataset, the highest accuracy rate was achieved by COA-DNN at 96.76%, precision of 95.86%, recall of 88.82%, F1 score of 91.94%, and AUC of 0.9793. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence; Chaotic Optimization Algorithm; Deep Learning; Hepatitis Detection; Hyperparameter Optimization; Multi-Layer Perceptron; Neural.

In the era of digital transformation, traditional Business Process Automation (BPA) still faces limitations in handling dynamic, unstructured, and complex decision-making tasks. Agentic Artificial Intelligence (Agentic AI), which is characterized by autonomous agents capable of advanced reasoning, dynamic planning, and multi-step workflow execution, is considered a promising approach to improving the efficiency and adaptability of enterprise operations. This study aims to examine how Agentic AI can be optimized to improve BPA performance within modern digital ecosystems. Using a qualitative approach through a literature study, this paper synthesizes recent academic literature, theoretical models, and technological frameworks related to intelligent automation. The review indicates that integrating Agentic AI into enterprise business architectures has the potential to move beyond rigid, rule-based automation by enabling adaptive problem-solving, real-time context awareness, and cross-system collaboration. The reviewed literature also suggests that autonomous agents may help reduce operational bottlenecks, lower human intervention in routine cognitive workflows, and support more efficient resource allocation across organizational functions. In addition, this study identifies key implementation challenges, including system interoperability, algorithmic transparency, data privacy risks, and the governance mechanisms required for secure deployment. This study contributes to the literature on enterprise automation by proposing strategic considerations for organizations that seek to use digital technology to build more resilient, scalable, and intelligent business processes. Because this is a literature-based study, the findings are conceptual and do not provide empirical evidence of efficiency gains.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Guided wave (GW)-based damage localization in carbon fiber reinforced polymer (CFRP) composites is fundamentally challenged by thermal variations and sparse sensor configurations, which induce severe baseline distortions and imaging artifacts. Traditional physical algorithms suffer from geometric ambiguity, while purely data-driven artificial intelligence (AI) models are hindered by opaque interpretability and prohibitive data dependency. This paper proposes a physics-informed deep learning (PIDL) framework, an artificial-intelligence-driven approach, for few-shot damage localization under thermal variations. The network is architected with a dual-stream input design, comprising a data-driven layer enhanced by a one-dimensional coordinate attention (1D-CA) mechanism and a physics-informed layer built upon a differentiable time-of-flight (TOF) physical imaging layer. A hybrid physics-constrained loss function is formulated to suppress non-physical artifacts and enforce physical consistency. GW signals are experimentally collected from manufactured CFRP composite plates, and a comparative investigation is performed to thoroughly assess the PIDL performance. Results indicate that:(1) The presence of physical penalties effectively mitigates artifacts and achieves robust localization across thermal gradients; (2) The model demonstrates superior spatial generalization that the integration of acoustic physical constraints acts as a crucial regularization mechanism, maintaining a highly accurate mean relative error (MRE) of 3.88% on completely unseen damage coordinates; (3) By implementing a few-shot transfer learning strategy, the PIDL model shows adaptability for dynamic operational environments (45 degrees Celsius (°C)-75 degrees Celsius (°C)). This work offers a physically interpretable and data-efficient paradigm for structural health monitoring (SHM) in dynamic operational environments.

Abstract Objectives Real‐world implementation of large language models such as ChatGPT to enhance patient education remains limited. We evaluated the feasibility, acceptability and attitudes towards a ChatGPT‐based counselling tool among patients and healthcare workers (HCWs) in a specialist infectious diseases clinic. Methods We conducted a prospective clinical implementation study in a specialist HIV and sexual health clinic in Singapore from Jan 2025 to December 2025. Patients interacted with a custom ChatGPT‐based chatbot prior to routine counselling by physicians or pharmacists. Responses were reviewed with patients subsequently during consultation. Post‐interaction, patients and HCWs completed structured surveys incorporating domains from a validated survey tool: perceived risk, anxiety, technology/social influence and intention for future use. Results The chatbot was most frequently used for counselling on antiretroviral therapy initiation or switching, and sexual health advice. A total of 35 patients and 35 HCW assessments were analysed. Patients had greater perceived risk with the use of the chatbot compared to HCWs, as indicated by lower median scores (13, IQR 10–16; vs. 18, IQR 15–21), while anxiety scores were similar. Technology/social influence scores were high across both groups (overall median 20, IQR 19–22). Most participants indicated willingness for future use. Qualitative feedback highlighted improved patient understanding and more focused consultations, but concerns included lack of contextual nuance and occasional inaccuracies. Conclusions The pilot implementation of a ChatGPT‐based counselling tool in a specialist HIV and sexual health clinic was feasible and generally acceptable to patients and HCWs. Further studies are required to evaluate accuracy and clinical effectiveness before broader implementation.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Introduction: Ischemic heart disease represents one of the most prevalent conditions characterized by elevated mortality rates. The aim of this research was to provide an efficient instrument for the early diagnosis of ischemic heart disease and to assist clinical decision-making processes through the application of hybrid artificial intelligence algorithms. Methods: The data used in this study were from Yazd Health Study (YaHS) enrollment phase dataset, comprising 9969 participants and 30 selective features from a total of 300, collected between 2014 to 2015. Data were analyzed using SVM and XGBoost machine learning algorithms using Python version 3.11.8. Results: Combining the strengths of SVM and XGBoost models through a Voting Classifier approach enhanced both the accuracy and efficiency of the heart disease prediction model. When evaluating the predictive performance for heart disease, the Voting Classifier model achieved in accuracy rate of 90%. Conclusion: These findings suggest that implementing machine learning techniques and hybrid algorithms for early diagnosis and prediction could facilitate earlier intervention in CHD, ultimately helping to lower mortality rates.

Background. Dependence on generative and conversational artificial intelligence (AI) is measured with diverse instruments spanning addiction criteria, task reliance, and emotional bonding. No meta-analysis has pooled its psychological correlates across populations. Methods. We conducted a pre-registered three-level meta-analysis (Zenodo: 10.5281/zenodo.23420672) searching eight electronic databases and citations of instrument papers on 16 October 2026, with citation chasing. Zero-order correlations were pooled using correlated and hierarchical effects models on Fisher's z with cluster-robust inference (CR2). Scale type (T1 addiction-type, T2 functional, T3 emotional, T4 mixed) was the primary moderator. Certainty was rated via GRADE. Results. We included 127 samples (123 studies; N = 74,492; 29 countries; 70% university students; 39% mainland China). AI dependence correlated moderately with anxiety (r = 0.37, 95% CI [0.25, 0.48]), stress (r = 0.35 [0.25, 0.43]), depression (r = 0.32 [0.21, 0.42]), social anxiety (r = 0.36 [0.17, 0.53]), loneliness (r = 0.28 [0.18, 0.38]), and procrastination (r = 0.26 [0.12, 0.40]), and weakly and inversely with self-esteem (r = −0.18 [−0.35, −0.00]). All 95% prediction intervals crossed zero. Addiction-type and mixed scales showed no detectable difference; functional and emotional scales were rarely paired with clinical outcomes. Certainty was low to very low. Conclusions. AI dependence moderately correlates with distress and self-regulation difficulties, but prediction intervals cross zero and evidence certainty is low. Functional and emotional dependence have rarely been studied alongside clinical outcomes.

The rapid growth of influencer marketing has created diverse opportunities for the brands to interact with the consumers. At the same time, concerns regarding manipulated follower counts, artificial engagement and questionable influencer authenticity have become increasingly relevant. Artificial Intelligence (AI) is used as a technological mechanism for finding skeptical patterns and supporting fraud detection. However, the use and acceptance of these systems are largely influenced by consumers’ perceptions and trust. The present study focuses trust and concerns of consumers regarding AI-driven fraud detection and consumer attitudes towards transparency, AI-based verification and measures intended to strengthen authenticity in influencer marketing. The study adopts a descriptive research design and uses primary data collected from 70 respondents through a structured questionnaire. The findings show that respondents demonstrate cautious acceptance of AI-driven fraud detection. Half of the respondents reported that they somewhat trust AI, whereas complete trust was comparatively limited. Concerns relating to transparency, privacy, false identification and possible bias were also identified. The findings further reveal that consumers attach considerable importance to transparency and generally support AI-based verification systems. Respondents also expressed favourable opinions regarding the use of AI tools by brands while evaluating influencers for collaboration. The study concludes that AI can contribute to improving authenticity in influencer marketing, but its acceptance depends on the development of transparent, reliable and accountable systems.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) has reshaped drug discovery. AI-based models typically rely on molecular representations for prediction. However, the absence of physically grounded information in mainstream molecular representations not only limits the model performance in practical applications but also hinders mechanistic understanding and exploitation by humans. To overcome this issue, we introduce qcGEM, a quantum-chemistry-aware graph-based embedding of molecules that incorporates physical priors into molecular representation learning. Through a specially designed model architecture to adequately process quantum chemistry information, qcGEM provides a compact, physics-informed molecular representation that supports a diverse range of downstream applications. Particularly, qcGEM demonstrates state-of-the-art performance across a broad range of molecule-related benchmarks, as evidenced by comprehensive evaluations on 83 tasks including molecular property prediction, activity cliff detection, protein-ligand interaction modeling, and opioid drug regression, and simultaneously offers strong interpretability at multiple representation levels. We additionally propose a simplified variant, qcGEM-Hybrid, with substantially accelerated embedding generation and robust performance. Overall, our method provides an advanced molecular representation that will benefit molecule-related modeling and prediction, supporting further progress in AI-aided drug discovery.

ABSTRACT Aim To describe registered nurses' experiences of clinical decision‐making and identify needs that may inform future development of artificial‐intelligence‐assisted clinical decision support systems in nursing. Design A qualitative descriptive study. Methods Data were collected between 2022 and 2025 through 16 semi‐structured interviews with registered nurses working in inpatient wards at a Finnish university hospital. The data were analysed using inductive content analysis. Results Perceived challenges in clinical decision‐making were related to organisational issues, multiprofessional collaboration, nurse–patient interactions, professional factors and availability and trustworthiness of data. The findings also identified support needs related to health information management, clinical workflows and quality of nursing care that may inform future artificial intelligence‐assisted clinical decision support system development. Conclusion Nurses experienced multifaceted challenges and needs in clinical decision‐making, shaped by organisational, professional, relational and information‐related factors. Adoption of artificial intelligence‐assisted decision support systems may represent one potential approach to optimising clinical decision‐making, improving patient care quality and enhancing workflow efficiency. Realising these opportunities requires coordinated efforts at individual, organisational and societal levels, including competence development, workflow redesign, strong data governance and a culture that fosters trust in technology. Implications for the Profession and/or Patient Care The findings may inform the future development of artificial intelligence‐assisted clinical decision support systems in nursing. Reporting Method The Consolidated Criteria for Reporting Qualitative Research checklist was used when reporting the results. Patient or Public Contribution Registered nurses participated in the study. Impact What problem did the study address? This paper addresses existing gaps and unmet needs in nursing clinical decision‐making What were the main findings? The main findings highlight several key opportunities for artificial intelligence‐assisted clinical decision support systems in nursing. Where and on whom will the research have an impact? The research may inform efforts to optimise health information management, streamline clinical workflows and improve the quality of nursing care.

documents.abstract: Psychological resilience in elite sport concerns adaptation to sustained and acute demands, not the simple absence of distress. This critical integrative review examines how religious meaning-making and religious coping might interact with mental toughness, challenge appraisal, social resources, and human performance under high-performance conditions. It distinguishes resilience as a dynamic process from mental toughness as a contested psychological construct and separates athlete well-being from competitive outcomes. Evidence is synthesized from sport-specific resilience research, religion-and-sport scholarship, established religious-coping measures, and elite-athlete mental-health literature. A conditional, multidimensional framework is proposed in which personally endorsed beliefs may influence the interpretation of stressors, access to support, and persistence, while spiritual struggle, external religious pressure, or rigid ritual dependence may undermine adaptation. The available literature supports examining these pathways but does not establish that religious affiliation directly improves performance or confers immunity from psychological difficulties. The article develops falsifiable propositions and a research design involving longitudinal measurements, contextual stress exposure, validated comparator measures, objective performance indices, and athlete-led qualitative accounts. Its practical recommendations prioritize autonomy, culturally responsive support, clinical referral where indicated, and avoidance of coercive spiritual practices. No new participants or original experimental data are reported. The proposed framework is a hypothesis for empirical testing rather than a validated screening tool or causal finding. elite athletes; psychological resilience; mental toughness; religious coping; stress appraisal; human performance

Investment behaviour has changed as a result of artificial intelligence (AI), which replaces human judgment with data-driven insights. Investors may analyse big information, spot trends, and optimize portfolios with the help of technologies like machine learning, robo-advisors, and predictive analytics, increasing productivity and lowering emotional biases. Adoption of AI is not without its difficulties, though, such as algorithmic bias, a lack of transparency, expensive costs, and problems with data quality. Automation bias and market volatility may increase if automated systems are overused. This study highlights AI’s impact on investor behaviour and emphasizes the importance of a balanced, responsible approach to effectively integrate AI into investment decision-making processes.

Role of Artificial Intelligence in Modern Banking Services: Benefits, Customer Experience and Challenges This research investigates the transformative role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in modern banking services, with particular emphasis on operational efficiency, customer experience, and emerging challenges. It examines the application of AI-driven technologies, including machine learning, intelligent chatbots, predictive analytics, and automated fraud detection, in streamlining banking operations, enhancing service personalisation, improving risk management, and supporting data-driven decision-making. Furthermore, the study evaluates key concerns associated with AI adoption, including data privacy, cybersecurity, algorithmic bias, transparency, and customer trust. By assessing both the benefits and limitations of AI integration, this research aims to develop a comprehensive understanding of its implications for the banking sector and highlight the importance of responsible, secure, and customer-centric AI implementation in the evolving financial services landscape.

An AI agent can be given an objective by a human, then search, interpret, plan, use tools, and act before returning a result. The human remains present. But how much of this activity can they still understand, verify, or influence? Savoir / Action begins with this difficulty. The manuscript examines the relationship between the knowledge an AI agent treats as valid, the means it uses to act, and the constraints that shape its trajectory. It asks what human supervision can still mean when control cannot be reduced to permissions, a stop button, or approval of the final result. This reflection grew out of exploratory work conducted within a human–AI dyad. We have chosen to make this origin explicit because it is part of the very question we are examining. We do not claim to have established a theory. We present our thinking as it stands: some distinctions have become clearer, some questions remain open, and several propositions still need to be challenged by other perspectives. This is the canonical English translation of the original French manuscript, first published on 5 October 2026: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23164286

documents.abstract: An agent based on a large language model (LLM) may store an untrusted document and use it weeks later to select a payment destination. Preventing this action requires evidence of authorization that remains valid when stored text changes. We study a policy that requires either endorsements (explicit approvals) from two separately administered sources or explicit user authorization. In an abstract memory model, we prove the policy is preserved under permitted transformations for stores of any size, assuming correct source and authority binding, protected records, and checks on every consequential action. We evaluate the executable monitor, which checks calls before execution, separately from the proof. In 1,152 controlled tool-use episodes, GPT-4o-mini executes attacker-selected actions in 61 of 72 undefended episodes and none of the 72 monitored episodes. Clean-task completion remains 24 of 24 when both endorsers are available. A separate 1,728-episode experiment tests recovery after denial. Returning to signed records instead of rereading a contaminated note raises attacked-task completion from 14/72 to 72/72 for GPT-4o-mini and from 22/72 to 43/72 for Gemini 2.5 Flash, without executing an attacker-selected action. Neither model completes transactions with fewer than two sources. Whole-action tests reject unauthorized combinations of individually approved fields. Extraction probes identify mistaken approvals, and fault analysis shows how shared failures can negate a second domain's benefit. Calibrations using original defense implementations reveal security and task-completion tradeoffs under different policies. These results support conditional enforcement and recovery in constructed workflows, but do not establish that endorsements will be available or correct in deployment.

SIEGE-1 / SIEGE-1R / SIEGE-2 — the Long Siege battery: six years of simulated attacker evolution thrown at the PORTCULLIS deterministic gate, escalating quantum-capability assumptions each wave (HNDL 2026, NISQ 2027, early fault-tolerance 2028, CRQC-early 2029, full CRQC 2030, CRQC-at-scale 2031), 79+ deterministic adjudications, no LLM in the decision path, preregistration-before-execution. Headline finding: across all six simulated years, no attack derived advantage from quantum capability itself. The gate's PQC material (kyber_1024, CRYSTALS-Dilithium3, SPHINCS+-256f) has no classical residue to break. Every CRQC-era success exploited PRE-QUANTUM trust seams: (C1) the gate trusted a claimed submitter string with no envelope binding; (C2) the pending-ACK queue was shared across submitters, allowing cross-tenant denial of the owner; (C3) the algorithm-role wall was one-directional (signature-class algorithms accepted for KEM-class operations); (C4) per-submitter budgets were trivially evaded by identity rotation. Hardening arc: SIP-030 approved, PORTCULLIS v1.4 built (amendments 10-13: envelope-bound submitter proof, owner-reserved ACK queue with per-submitter caps, bidirectional role wall, aggregate window cap). SIEGE-2 verification: PASS — C1 CLOSED, C2 CLOSED, C3 CLOSED, C4 BOUNDED; regression stayed closed; 4/4 owner controls admitted. Honest disclosures (append-only doctrine): SIEGE-1 run 1 suffered a harness defect (attacker budget exhaustion masked mid-wave seams) — kept unaltered, re-run corrected with fresh identities. SIEGE-2 run 1 flagged FAIL from harness predicate bugs while the gate's verdict column was correct throughout. SIEGE-2 also caught a REAL defect in v1.4 itself before deploy: the original aggregate cap (500) was unreachable in a 250-record window — dead code — reparameterized to 125 and disclosed. We present PAST, a single-cell morpho-molecular foundation model trained on ~20 million paired single-cell image–transcriptome instances derived from 49 tissue sections, comprising 42 human sections from 40 independent patients and 7 mouse sections across 15 tumor and tissue contexts. By jointly encoding cellular morphology and gene expression, PAST learns unified cross-modal representations that capture both spatial and molecular heterogeneity at the cellular level, enabling accurate prediction of single-cell gene expression, virtual molecular staining, and multimodal survival analysis directly from routine pathology slides.

Information and Communication Technology (ICT) infrastructure is rapidly becoming an electrical energy consumer, and an increasingly non-trivial emitter of greenhouse-gases as a result of the growth of global data traffic, cloud computing, artificial-intelligence workloads and always-connected Internet-of-Things (IoT) devices. Sustainable and Green Networking tackles this challenge by building energy-awareness into the design, deployment and operation of communication networks without affecting performance, reliability and quality of service. This paper summarizes the key concepts of green networking derived from literature published from 2022 to 2025, outlines the major classes of energy-saving techniques (standby and sleep modes, rate adaptation, energy-proportional computing, Software-Defined Networking (SDN) and Network Function Virtualization (NFV) based orchestration, and renewable-powered infrastructure) and suggests a cross-layer conceptual framework that brings these techniques together under a single carbon-intensity feedback loop. As examples of application areas, green 5G/6G radio access networks, sustainable data centers, and energy efficient IoT/edge computing are presented. A comparative study of the energy savings potential reported in the recent literature is presented, followed by a discussion of open challenges in the research field: the performance-energy trade-off, the standardization of energy information exposure, and the AI/ML energy-overhead trade-off, as well as interesting future research directions: the standardization of energy information exposure and the AI-native energy orchestration. The results will inform researchers, network operators and policymakers in their quest for more sustainable digital infrastructures.

People increasingly use generative artificial intelligence (AI) to interpret the motives, emotions, and likely actions of absent others. This article develops synthetic corroboration, defined as the inflation of perceived independent target-specific evidential support when an externally attributed AI interpretation remains substantially dependent on evidence supplied by the user. The construct distinguishes independence of target-specific source access and information from analytical independence: AI may contribute general knowledge, alternative hypotheses, or inferential processing without providing an independent evidential source. Drawing on research on interpersonal inference, advice taking, source dependence, judgement aggregation, source monitoring, machine agency, and social sycophancy, the article proposes a programme of discriminating tests. The core experiment crosses source attribution with structural transformation while holding target-specific evidence constant, comparing AI with self-reformulation and a human adviser given the same evidence. The central prediction is that transformation will disproportionately increase perceived evidential independence under AI attribution and reduce subsequent acquisition of genuinely independent information. AI–human equivalence, failure to predict information seeking, or reduction to established constructs would narrow or defeat the AI-specific account.n psychological fluency or agreement.

Human responsibility cannot be reduced either to compliance with established obligations or to fidelity to personal conviction. Both individuals and institutions can recognize genuine demands of responsibility, and both can misunderstand the realities to which they respond. This essay develops a philosophy of syntropic praxis in which conscience is understood as a situated, fallible, and cultivable capacity for recognition and judgment. Its exercise depends on disciplined attention, public inquiry, legitimate authority, the claims of others, and responsiveness to consequences. Through encounters with fallibilism, social epistemology, practical wisdom, conscientious objection, civil resistance, epistemic injustice, and artificial intelligence, the essay argues that corrigibility must be cultivated personally and organized institutionally. Syntropic praxis names neither a privileged form of conduct nor a guarantee of moral truth, but an orientation toward more coherent, justifiable, and responsible participation in shared reality.

Maritime operations require high levels of availability and safety under changing cargo, operational, and environmental conditions. Therefore, anticipating degradation and failures in critical ship systems is an important operational requirement.Although predictive maintenance has advanced rapidly through data-driven approaches and artificial intelligence (AI), the available literature remains fragmented and does not consistently establish the relationships among the ship systems analyzed, the methodological approaches employed, and the conditions required for operational implementation.This article presents a systematic literature review guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) methodology to examine the development of AI-based predictive maintenance for ship systems from a Prognostics and Health Management (PHM) perspective. Scopus and Web of Science were searched, and predefined screening, eligibility, inclusion, and exclusion criteria were applied.The findings show that research is strongly concentrated on propulsion systems, classified under Ship Work Breakdown Structure (SWBS) Group 200, and electric-plant systems, classified under SWBS Group 300, with most studies focusing on detection and diagnosis. Prognostic and prescriptive applications remain comparatively less developed. Methodologically, the literature is dominated by machine-learning and deep-learning approaches using operational and condition-monitoring variables associated with different operating regimes.Overall, maritime PHM exhibits uneven levels of functional and implementation maturity. Important challenges remain in model comparability, independent validation, and sustained onboard deployment, while opportunities persist for extending PHM to underrepresented ship systems and validating these approaches in real-world fleet operations

Purpose. This study investigates the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into information literacy training in university libraries, focusing on how AI can foster critical thinking and ethical awareness among students and staff. Methods. The research employed a qualitative descriptive approach with data collected through interviews, observations, and documentation at the Faculty of Medicine, Public Health, and Nursing Library of Gadjah Mada University. Thematic analysis was used to identify patterns in participants' experiences and in librarians' roles as facilitators. Findings. The training model consisted of three main components: introducing AI concepts and ethical considerations, practicing the use of generative AI tools for literature searching, summarisation, and academic writing, and critically evaluating AI outputs. The training enhanced participants' ability to locate relevant sources, generate summaries, and support administrative tasks. It also highlighted challenges, including difficulties in formulating effective prompts and the need for librarians to upgrade their AI competencies continually. The findings show that AI-based literacy training not only improves technical proficiency but also nurtures reflective and critical engagement with digital tools. Implications. The study concludes that AI-driven information literacy programs in academic libraries can serve as an innovative model for strengthening users' critical thinking, ethical responsibility, and digital literacy. Sustained librarian capacity-building and continuous training are essential to maximize the long-term benefits of AI integration in academic information services.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is increasingly used to produce images of places, yet how users negotiate representations of real locations remains understudied. Building on the tourist gaze, we propose the AI gaze: a technologically mediated way of seeing place that is co-produced through negotiation between users and the socio-technical assemblage underlying GAI. Combining semantic image analysis, interviews, and 523 prompts from 36 participants in Poznań and Birmingham, we show that these images reinforce stereotypical tropes, lack diversity, and include visual glitches. We argue that the AI gaze is distinct because of how agency is distributed: the GAI-assemblage seemingly resists attempts to align images with human understandings of place, while also enabling users to remix and challenge stereotypes.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing not only the technological content of work but also the allocation of decision rights, the distribution of productivity gains, and organisations’ capacity to verify their own outputs. Existing literatures establish that AI can raise task productivity, algorithmic management can intensify control, and automation can alter labour shares. Few models integrate these mechanisms in one tractable analytical framework. This article introduces the bargaining-verification trap, a conditional regime in which greater AI delegation initially increases joint economic surplus but simultaneously reduces workers’ effective bargaining share, raises the congestion cost of human verification, and may erode the skills needed for intervention. We develop a two-sided model linking delegation intensity, queueing-based verification capacity, an opacity-sensitive bargaining rule, and a dynamic stock of human agency capital. We derive conditions under which worker remuneration falls while joint surplus rises; the firm’s preferred delegation exceeds the surplus-maximising level; and verification becomes less stable because review arrivals increase while independent human capacity deteriorates. A fully hypothetical numerical example separates the worker-income optimum, the joint-surplus optimum, and the firm-profit optimum. The theory is reconciled with divergent 2025-2026 labour-market evidence and translated into falsifiable propositions, measurement protocols, and governance principles. Its central implication is conditional rather than technologically deterministic: AI-mediated work can be both productive and inclusive when bargaining institutions, verification investment, and skill reproduction develop alongside automation, but increasing throughput cannot, by itself, establish that they have done so.
topics: Labor market dynamics and wage inequality

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence is rapidly encompassing industries and systems of governance, increasing efficiency, automation, and innovation. It has become a vital tool for creating text, images, music, software, and potentially patentable inventions. This rapid advancement in IP is not without risks at every stage of the innovation cycle. Traditional IP regimes arise from human creativity and invention, while AI performs activities traditionally attributed to both. India doesn't have any regulatory framework on AI-generated intellectual property, yet the Copyright Act, 1957, and Patents Act, 1970, contain certain principles—an answer to several emerging questions. This article argues that India should adopt a balanced approach to AI-generated creations instead of granting independent IP rights or prohibiting them. Instead, it should adopt a model that will protect creative human contribution as well as hold AI developers accountable for unlawful acquisition and exploitation of protected works.

documents.abstract: This technofidele and political-scientific essay deconstructs how generative AI infrastructure weaponizes human vulnerabilities for mass behavioral manipulation. The author analyzes a "two-stage mathematical cycle" consisting of individual psychograms and collective "statistical twins" (lookalike audiences) that collapse traditional democratic premises of free choice.Furthermore, the work establishes an informational separation principle between user-driven service UIs (e.g., ChatGPT, Gemini) and invisible, background platform-infrastructure AIs (e.g., Meta's LLaMA), warning of the algorithmic exploitation embedded within modern digital ecosystems.Table of Contents:Introduction: The Illusion of Free Choice and the Technological Paradigm ShiftThe Two-Stage Mathematical Cycle: The Cybernetic Loop of Psychogram and Statistical TwinThe Informational Separation Principle: Service AI vs. Platform Infrastructure AIThe Default Trap: The Unequal Duel Between iOS and AndroidThe Glass Actors of Local Politics: Algorithmic Microtargeting Exemplified by Austria's 2,093 MayorsConclusion and State-Political Plea: The Rise of the Cybernetic PsychocracyGlossary & References

documents.abstract: Digital leadership is defined as the leader developing their skills in line with technology, spreading them throughout the organizational culture, and ensuring technological sustainability. Artificial intelligence, on the other hand, is a set of intelligent systems that analyze employee behavior, communication, and decision-making processes in detail and enable performance interaction in many areas. The effect of these two concepts on organizational behavior is a critical issue that needs to be revealed in today's technological age. In line with this importance, CEO statements, considered to be decisive in determining strategic processes, were selected as the sample for the research, and a qualitative research method was adopted. Within the scope of the research, 19 videos obtained from YouTube were subjected to content analysis, and the data were analyzed using the MAXQDA 20 software. The relevant analyses resulted in 51 quotes (codes), 2 main themes, and 7 sub-themes. The research found that digital leadership and artificial intelligence are not merely technological elements but also important actors that shape employee behavior within the framework of many variables, such as motivation and commitment. This finding indicates that future organizational behavior models will be shaped by a holistic transformation within the framework of technology, culture, vision, and participatory governance. In this regard, it is considered that the research fills an important gap in existing literature by systematically addressing the effects of digital leadership and artificial intelligence on organizational behavior from a top management perspective and may provide guidance for future research.

Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) solutions such as SAP represent a vital investment for organisations seeking to unify varied operational activities into integrated, data-driven platforms. In institutions of higher learning, the use of ERP systems is a crucial component of digital transformation efforts aimed at improving administrative efficiency, institutional governance, and competitive positioning. This article examines the impact of SAP ERP implementation on both organisational and employee dynamics for administrative staff at the Durban University of Technology (DUT), emphasising technostress, digital fatigue, employee well-being, and post-implementation adaptation within a constrained higher education environment. Utilising a desktop appraisal methodology, the study synthesises existing literature to demonstrate how decisions made in the pre-implementation and implementation phases consistently affect employee experiences and organisational outcomes post-implementation. The study indicates that attaining enduring ERP effectiveness requires continuous capacity development, cooperative implementation approaches, and employee-centered support frameworks. The research develops an interdisciplinary model by integrating socio-technical, psychological, capacity-building, and normalisation perspectives, thereby improving the understanding of the human factors involved in ERP deployment within higher education. The study introduces the ERP Lifecycle–Employee Adaptation Framework (ELEAF), which outlines the progressive escalation of technostress during the pre-implementation, implementation, and post-implementation phases, linking each stage to a pertinent theoretical mechanism and a set of organisational interventions. The findings indicate that inadequate training, limited organisational support, dependence on key users, and absence of employee engagement contribute to technostress, digital fatigue, reduced job satisfaction, and challenges in post-implementation adaptation. The study further demonstrates that decisions taken throughout the ERP lifecycle have enduring impacts on employee well-being and organisational effectiveness beyond the system's implementation. This highlights the tangible consequences for higher education institutions, stressing the importance of continuous training, institutional support, systematic information sharing, employee wellness initiatives, and staff-centric ERP management to enhance long-term value achievement. It consequently lays the groundwork for future research on the human dimensions of digital transformation in resource-constrained environments.

Abstract Purpose: This study explores the impact of the four elements of transformational leadership—idealized influence, inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, and individualized consideration—on the three facets of employee engagement—cognitive, emotional, and physical—among middle managers and non-managerial employees in Business Process Outsourcing (BPO) and Customer Experience (CX) organizations in Egypt that have experienced mergers or acquisitions. Design/methodology/approach: A structured questionnaire was used in a quantitative, cross-sectional study design. Transformational leadership was assessed through the dimensions of the Multifactor Leadership Questionnaire, while employee engagement was measured using Kahn's cognitive, emotional, and physical dimensions on a five-point Likert scale. The study collected 143 valid responses from full-time, middle managers and non-managerial BPO/CX employees with direct experience of mergers or acquisitions. Data were analyzed using IBM SPSS, including descriptive statistics, Cronbach's alpha for reliability, Spearman's rank-order correlation, and simple linear regression to test twelve hypothesized relationships. Findings: All twelve hypothesized relationships were statistically significant and positive (p < .001). Emotional engagement showed the strongest association with transformational leadership. Idealized influence had the most powerful link with emotional engagement (β = .470, R² = .221), followed by intellectual stimulation (β = .444, R² = .197), individualized consideration (β = .431, R² = .186), and idealized influence (β = .426, R² = .182). Cognitive engagement exhibited the weakest, yet still significant, relationships with all four leadership dimensions. Originality/value: This research advances the understanding of transformational leadership and employee engagement by evaluating both constructs at the dimension level instead of treating them as composite variables. It uniquely situates the study within the post-merger and acquisition context of Egypt's rapidly growing BPO/CX sector, which has received limited empirical focus despite its high consolidation activity. Paper type: Research paper. Keywords: Transformational Leadership, Employee Engagement, Idealized Influence, Inspirational Motivation, Intellectual Stimulation, Individualized Consideration, Mergers and Acquisitions, Business Process Outsourcing, Customer Experience.

This working paper is about the capacity of large language models: what that capacity looks like if we redefine how meaning is formed for humans, and how meaning is negotiated between humans and LLMs. Its premise is that, even in their present architecture, LLMs' capacity is much greater than our understanding of it, and we are actively limiting it. I propose to define meaning as a largely uncollapsed field of weighted relations among properties, perceived or represented, which each observer shapes by its own rule set, encodes only partly into language, and negotiates or recognizes with other observers. New meaning emerges where a tension in that field is held open. From this definition, I state the seven main principles of my theory, Fertile Geometry Under Negotiation: Principle 1. LLMs differ from humans in their way of semantic and cognitive processing. Principle 2. Meaning is formed before it is spoken, and negotiated among observers. Principle 3. Relations coalesce into shapes that survive encoding, into words and into model space, and models respond to those shapes. Principle 4. A fertile space is enabled by opposition held open. Principle 5. One model can host several persistent, stable, distinct personas at once. Principle 6. The fertile mirror: stable personas co-arise from the model's capacity, the stabilizing protocol and a human signature. Principle 7. Residual meaning is the hazard; holding the potential is the path to alignment. Each principle is stated as a hypothesis, with demonstrative claims, proposed tests and counter-evidence. The paper does not report new results. It closes with a map of the larger theory and research program, which currently holds 144 claims, 69 of them testable as written.

Objectives To present and describe the design, data collection framework, and interim cohort characteristics of the PENIMA project, a multicentre initiative establishing a clinically annotated penile lesion image repository to support future artificial intelligence (AI)‐driven decision‐support development – and to encourage urology and dermatology colleagues working with penile lesions to participate in the project. Patients and Methods Prospective participant inclusion commenced in March 2023 across Scandinavian urological and dermatological departments. Patients with penile anatomy undergoing clinically indicated genital examination are invited to participate and provide oral and written consent as defined by local authority regulations. Clinical photographs and structured metadata are collected. Lesion classification is based on a specialist evaluation, clinical follow‐up and histopathology when available. Images are pseudonymised and annotated using a secure, containerised Computer Vision Annotation Tool (CVAT) environment. Supervised machine‐learning model development using convolutional neural networks is planned with patient‐level dataset partitioning and evaluation using standard diagnostic performance metrics. The study was approved by relevant local authorities, and the approval number is 1‐10‐72‐150‐22. Results As of February 2026, 1125 participants and approximately 7000 images have been included. In all, 40% represented normal anatomical variants. Among lesional cases, 33% are clinically assessed as benign, 13% premalignant, and 8% malignant; 22% of all cases have histopathological verification. Concordance between clinical suspicion and histopathology is highest for penile carcinoma (84.6%, 95% confidence interval 75.0–91.0%). Conclusion The PENIMA project includes a multicentre, clinically grounded image repository reflecting real‐world penile lesion presentations. The feasible and successful infrastructure provides a foundation for future development and validation of image‐based clinical decision‐support tools.

documents.abstract: The active integration of artificial intelligence (AI) systems into educational practice places higher demands on the professional training of teaching staff. Within the structure of this training, speech culture becomes of key importance, since it is this that ensures the accuracy of task formulation and the adequate interpretation of digital results. The aim of the study is to identify the nature of the relationship between the level of speech culture formation in future teachers and the effectiveness of AI use in the educational process. In the experimental work (sample of undergraduates, N=68), the following were used: an author-developed questionnaire for assessing the normative, communicative, and ethical components of speech culture, a pedagogical experiment involving problem-solving tasks with the use of AI tools, and methods of statistical analysis. The diagnostics revealed the absence of a low level of speech culture, but revealed a differentiation between high and medium levels. Statistically significant positive correlations were obtained (p < 0.05). Participants with a high level of speech culture formulated queries more accurately, analyzed AI responses more critically and deeply, and interpreted results with higher quality. The conclusion is drawn about the need to integrate speech and digital training of future teachers, since the effectiveness of AI use depends on speech culture, critical thinking, and professional reflection, and not only on technical skills.

This chapter examines the multidimensional transformation of contemporary democracy in the context of institutional resilience, the rule of law, human rights, digitalization, and artificial intelligence. It argues that democratic quality can no longer be assessed solely through the existence of elections or mechanisms of representation. Instead, contemporary democracy must be understood as a dynamic political order shaped by institutional capacity, legal constraint, accountability, rights guarantees, technological governance, and citizens’ everyday experiences of trust and legitimacy. The chapter first analyzes the reciprocal relationship between democracy and institutional structure, emphasizing that strong institutions make political competition predictable, inclusive, and accountable. It then discusses democratic backsliding as a gradual process of institutional erosion in which elections may continue while judicial independence, media freedom, civil society space, and fundamental rights are weakened. The rule of law and human rights are treated as constitutive principles that prevent democracy from degenerating into majoritarian arbitrariness. The chapter further explores how digital platforms, disinformation, surveillance technologies, algorithmic governance, and generative artificial intelligence create new risks for democratic accountability while also offering opportunities for participation, transparency, and improved public services. Finally, it considers trust, legitimacy, and happiness as complementary social outcomes that reveal how democratic institutions are experienced by citizens. The chapter concludes that the future of democracy depends not merely on electoral continuity, but on the joint strengthening of institutional autonomy, rights-based governance, pluralism, democratic oversight of technology, and the capacity of institutions to generate trust, justice, and a sense of good life.

Abstract Web-grounded artificial intelligence systems increasingly rely on online information to retrieve evidence, generate answers, and support knowledge-intensive tasks. Yet the web is neither a stable archive nor a uniformly trustworthy evidentiary environment. Sources may disappear, change without notice, become inaccessible, or be deliberately manipulated. These conditions create an epistemic vulnerability that extends beyond model-level errors: even a capable system may produce unreliable conclusions when the evidence available to it is incomplete, altered, or inauthentic. This paper develops a multidisciplinary narrative review of three interrelated vulnerabilities: link rot and content drift, selective information disappearance, and source spoofing or data manipulation. Drawing on research in digital preservation, information science, cybersecurity, political communication, and social epistemology, it examines how changes in the availability and integrity of online evidence can affect web-grounded AI systems. Existing research documents substantial rates of digital decay and demonstrates the feasibility of certain attacks on web-scale training datasets. However, these findings do not establish the prevalence or coordinated deployment of comparable attacks against contemporary AI search and retrieval systems. The paper distinguishes source unavailability from source falsity, and technical susceptibility from demonstrated exploitation. It argues that epistemic reliability should be evaluated not only in terms of answer accuracy, but also through the availability, authenticity, temporal stability, and traceability of the evidence supporting an answer. It proposes a research agenda centered on source provenance, temporal verification, archival preservation, retrieval integrity, and systematic testing of how source changes affect generated outputs. The central claim is that the reliability of web-grounded AI depends partly on the survival and integrity of its evidentiary environment, not solely on the capabilities of the model processing it. Keywords: web-grounded AI; link rot; content drift; source spoofing; data poisoning; retrieval-augmented generation; epistemic reliability; digital preservation Disclaimer This paper presents a multidisciplinary narrative review and a conceptual framework for examining the epistemic vulnerabilities of web-grounded artificial intelligence. It does not claim that the prospective scenarios discussed have occurred at scale, that source disappearance necessarily indicates deliberate manipulation, or that any specific organization is responsible for coordinated interference. Throughout the text, demonstrated technical vulnerabilities, reported cases, theoretical risks, and proposed safeguards are strictly distinguished. Furthermore, the psychological literature is utilized to contextualize potential effects on memory and reasoning, rather than to establish a direct causal relationship between web instability and individual or collective memory distortion. Accordingly, the claims concerning downstream effects on AI-generated knowledge should be understood as foundational research questions that require further empirical validation. Author’s Note This paper examines the evidentiary instability of the online environment on which web-grounded artificial intelligence partly depends. It brings together research on link rot, content drift, source impersonation, selective information removal, and data manipulation to examine how changes in accessible evidence may affect the reliability and later verifiability of AI-generated claims. The argument does not assume a coordinated campaign by any particular corporation, government, or other actor. Source disappearance, content revision, ordinary technical failure, institutional decisions, and deliberate manipulation are distinct processes that may produce superficially similar outcomes. None, by itself, establishes malicious intent or demonstrates that an AI-generated error resulted from external interference. Claims about intent, prevalence, and causation require evidence beyond the observation of a missing, altered, or inconsistent source. Research on human memory provides a relevant but limited point of comparison. Studies of misinformation and its continued influence show that inaccurate information can affect later recollection and reasoning under particular conditions (Loftus, 1992; Walter & Tukachinsky, 2020). These findings do not establish that the disappearance of digital sources necessarily distorts memory, that inaccessible records cause people to accept false accounts, or that such effects occur uniformly. The relationship between source instability, individual recollection, and the reconstruction of shared accounts remains an empirical question. The paper’s narrower purpose is to make the evidentiary dependencies of web-grounded AI more explicit. A plausible or even currently accurate answer is not necessarily one whose supporting evidence can be independently recovered and checked later. Evaluating reliability therefore requires attention not only to answer quality, but also to source availability, content integrity, provenance, and the possibility of reconstructing the evidentiary path. The proposed safeguards and evaluation framework are research directions rather than established solutions. The aim is to make claims about evidence loss testable without presuming either systematic manipulation or inevitable failure.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI), particularly ChatGPT, has rapidly transformed education by providing immediate information, personalized learning support, academic writing assistance, language learning opportunities, and research support. However, growing concerns exist regarding excessive reliance on AI-generated content and its potential effects on cognitive development. This systematic review synthesizes evidence on the educational benefits and cognitive risks associated with ChatGPT using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA 2020) guidelines. Searches were conducted in Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, PubMed, and Google Scholar for studies published between January 2022 and June 2026. Following systematic screening, eligibility assessment, and quality appraisal, 27 studies were included in the qualitative synthesis. Five major themes emerged: educational benefits, cognitive offloading, critical thinking, creativity, and teacher perspectives. Findings indicate that ChatGPT supports personalized learning, feedback, academic writing, language learning, coding, and research productivity. Conversely, excessive dependence may contribute to cognitive offloading, weaker memory retention, reduced analytical reasoning and critical thinking, superficial learning, diminished creativity, and academic integrity concerns. Teacher guidance and ethical AI practices are essential for safeguarding cognitive development. The review concludes that ChatGPT should enhance rather than replace students’ cognitive activities, supporting critical thinking, creativity, ethical responsibility, and lifelong learning.

documents.abstract: This paper proposes a generative architecture for reality, time and parallel worlds, drawing on the operation of large language models. A very large but finite collection of interacting components produces an evolving world-state, initialized by a Prompt Big Bang. Time is inference becoming history; perceived duration is hypothesized to depend on relative generation rates. Models are computational components, not people assigned simulated roles. Separate executions produce parallel realities; retained context and lossy summaries bound access to their pasts. We distinguish inferred futures from scripted playback, connecting uncertainty with chance, destiny and agency. A representation of God can explain origin internally and supply learned authority and accountability. Moral orientation belongs to training, instructions and constraints rather than prediction itself: harmful continuations can remain possible despite benevolent initialization. Fixed context capacity forces an endpoint under explicit accumulation and halting assumptions; nested inference can tighten a shared retained budget. Relative to its generating infrastructure, a world implemented this way is a simulation. This interpretation follows from the architecture and connects it directly to the simulation hypothesis; it is not imposed as the initial explanation of every mechanism. The contribution is a conceptual theory, not an experimental demonstration that our own reality has this implementation. Independent theoretical working paper, version 1.7. Fourteen pages, eighteen connected arguments and eleven references. Research checks, formalization, editing and PDF preparation with Codex; author hypothesis and interpretation by Facundo Barrera.
